metadata.title: Response-adaptive targeting for multi-treatment experiments (RemyDegenne/alpha-rar Lean blueprint)

extraction_notes.note: The blueprint's 'Lean remark', 'Formalization note', 'Formalization status' and 'Recommended formalization path' paragraphs and the part/chapter overviews describe the Lean development, not mathematics; they get no nodes (except the empty-set convention for the hitting time, which a lemma cites).

Most long proofs end with an \emph{Formalization.} paragraph, which the parser reports as an author label (often together with an adjacent \texttt{...} label); these became 'other' proof steps, nested under the Formalization step or split off as a heading-only step when the paragraph is one sentence.
These two proofs are separated from their results by a remark and a formalization note, so syntax gives no proves target; the proves edge to the preceding result was added by hand (inferred, 0.8).
definition or problem: the homogeneity test is the decision problem of Chapter 9, but the sentence mainly introduces H_0 and H_1 used by later nodes.
remark or open_problem: it ends by calling the chasing-design sparse CLT 'genuinely open', but it is mainly a discussion of the hypothesis' scope, so it stays a remark.

origin: classical results restated in Part II (Hartman-Wintner, martingale SLLN/CLT/LIL, Kronecker, Slutsky, Cochran, chi-square facts) are marked external even though the blueprint re-proves them; the blueprint's own decomposition lemmas are marked paper.

metadata.extraction_comment: This is a Lean blueprint of a paper on response-adaptive randomization: Part I proves the paper's theorems, Part II re-derives the probabilistic prerequisites (martingale SLLN, LIL, CLT, Cochran) as small lemmas with proof sketches.

nodes.statement: Throughout, everything lives on a fixed probability space $(\Omega, \filt, \Prob)$.
nodes.name: Underlying probability space

nodes.statement: We work with $K \geq 2$ treatments (``arms''), indexed by $[K] := \{1, \dots, K\}$.
nodes.name: Treatment arms [K]

nodes.statement:
For each patient $m \ge 1$, the \emph{assignment vector}
$X_m = (X_{m,1}, \dots, X_{m,K})$ takes values in $\{0,1\}^K$ and satisfies
$\sum_{k=1}^K X_{m,k} = 1$. The event $\{X_{m,k} = 1\}$ means that patient $m$ is
assigned to arm $k$.
nodes.name: Assignment vector
nodes.label: def:assignment

nodes.statement:
For each arm $k \in [K]$, $\{\xi_{m,k} : m \ge 1\}$ is a sequence of i.i.d.\
real random variables, the potential responses of patients on treatment $k$.
The parameter of interest for arm $k$ is the mean
$\theta_k := \E[\xi_{1,k}]$, and $\Params = (\theta_1, \dots, \theta_K) \in \R^K$.
We write $V_k := \Var[\xi_{1,k}]$ for the variance of the response of arm $k$.
nodes.name: Responses and parameters
nodes.label: def:responses

nodes.statement:
The number of patients assigned to arm $k$ up to time $n$ is
\[
  N_{n,k} := \sum_{j=1}^n X_{j,k}, \qquad N_n := (N_{n,1}, \dots, N_{n,K}).
\]
The vector $N_n / n$ is the \emph{observed allocation proportion} at time $n$.
nodes.name: Allocation counts
nodes.label: def:counts

nodes.statement:
For all $n \ge 1$, $\sum_{k=1}^K N_{n,k} = n$, and hence
$\sum_{k=1}^K \frac{N_{n,k}}{n} = 1$.
nodes.name: Counts sum to time
nodes.label: lem:counts_sum

nodes.statement: Immediate from $\sum_{k=1}^K X_{j,k} = 1$ and summing over $j \le n$.
nodes.name: Proof of Counts sum to time
nodes.statement_short: Sum the one-hot assignment identity over patients.

nodes.statement:
$\filt_m := \sigma\big((X_i, \xi_i)_{1 \le i \le m}\big)$ is the filtration
generated by the assignments and observed outcomes of the first $m$ patients,
with $\filt_0$ the trivial $\sigma$-algebra.
nodes.name: Filtration
nodes.label: def:filtration

nodes.statement:
A \emph{response-adaptive randomization (RAR) procedure} is a sequence
$(p_m)_{m \ge 1}$ of $\filt_m$-measurable random vectors taking values in the
probability simplex
\[
  \simplex_K := \Big\{ p \in [0,1]^K : \sum_{k=1}^K p_k = 1 \Big\},
\]
such that the assignment $X_{m+1}$ is drawn conditionally on $\filt_m$ according
to $p_m$:
\[
  \Prob(X_{m+1} = k \mid \filt_m) = p_{m,k}, \qquad k \in [K].
\]
nodes.name: RAR procedure
nodes.label: def:rar

nodes.statement:
A \emph{target function} is a map $\Target : \hilb \to \simplex_K$ defined on an
open domain $\hilb \subseteq \R^K$, written
$\Target(z) = (\Target_1(z), \dots, \Target_K(z))$ with
$\sum_{k=1}^K \Target_k(z) = 1$. The \emph{target allocation} is
$v := \Target(\Params)$. A RAR procedure is an \emph{adaptive targeting
mechanism} if $N_n/n \to v$.
nodes.name: Target function and target allocation
nodes.label: def:target

nodes.statement:
Given initial values $\theta_{0,k} \in \R$, the sequential estimator of
$\theta_k$ at stage $m$ is
\[
  \hat{\theta}_{m,k} := \frac{\sum_{j=1}^m X_{j,k}\, \xi_{j,k} + \theta_{0,k}}{N_{m,k} + 1}.
\]
We write $\estParams_m := (\hat{\theta}_{m,1}, \dots, \hat{\theta}_{m,K})$.
nodes.name: Sequential estimator
nodes.statement_short: Regularized running mean of arm k's responses.
nodes.label: def:estimator

nodes.statement:
The plug-in estimator of the target allocation is
$\estTarget_m := \Target(\estParams_m)$, with components $\hat{\rho}_{m,k}$.
It is well defined once $\estParams_m \in \hilb$, which is guaranteed by
Condition~\ref{def:condB}.
nodes.name: Plug-in target
nodes.label: def:plugin_target

nodes.statement:
An estimator $\hat{\theta}_{m,k}$ of $\theta_k$ admits a \emph{Bahadur
representation} if
\[
  \hat{\theta}_{m,k} = \frac{1}{N_{m,k}}\sum_{j=1}^m X_{j,k}\, \xi_{j,k}
    + o\!\big(N_{m,k}^{-1/2}\big), \qquad m \to \infty.
\]
nodes.name: Bahadur representation
nodes.label: def:bahadur

nodes.statement:
On the event $\{N_{m,k} \to \infty\}$, the estimator of
Definition~\ref{def:estimator} admits the Bahadur representation of
Definition~\ref{def:bahadur}. The formalized statement \texttt{estimator\_sub\_eq} is the sharper
\emph{exact} error identity
\[
  \hat{\theta}_{m,k} - \theta_k = \frac{Q_{m,k} + (\theta_{0,k} - \theta_k)}{N_{m,k} + 1},
\]
which holds pathwise for every $m$ (with $N_{m,k}+1 \ne 0$, automatic for $\{0,1\}$-indicators) and
from which the $o(N^{-1/2})$ Bahadur form is immediate.
nodes.name: The sequential estimator is Bahadur
nodes.label: lem:estimator_bahadur

nodes.statement:
The numerator of $\hat{\theta}_{m,k} - \theta_k = \frac{\sum_j X_{j,k}\xi_{j,k} + \theta_{0,k}}{N_{m,k}
+ 1} - \theta_k$ is $\sum_j X_{j,k}\xi_{j,k} + \theta_{0,k} - \theta_k(N_{m,k}+1) = (\sum_j
X_{j,k}\xi_{j,k} - \theta_k N_{m,k}) + (\theta_{0,k} - \theta_k) = Q_{m,k} + (\theta_{0,k} -
\theta_k)$, giving the exact identity. On $\{N_{m,k}\to\infty\}$ the offset
$\frac{\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k}{N_{m,k}+1} = O(N_{m,k}^{-1}) = o(N_{m,k}^{-1/2})$, which is the Bahadur
form.
nodes.name: Proof of The sequential estimator is Bahadur
nodes.statement_short: Algebraic rewriting of the estimator numerator gives the exact error identity; the offset is O(1/N).

nodes.statement:
Condition~\textbf{A} holds if for every arm $k \in [K]$ the response satisfies
$\E|\xi_{1,k}|^2 < \infty$ (equivalently $V_k < \infty$).
nodes.name: Condition A: second moments
nodes.label: def:condA

nodes.statement:
For each arm $k$, let $V_k^{\mathrm{att}}$ be the set of all values attainable by
the estimator $\hat{\theta}_{n,k}$, over all $n$ and all realizations of the
responses $\{\xi_{j,k}\}$, and set $I_k := \{\theta_k\} \cup V_k^{\mathrm{att}}$.
(The formalized \texttt{AlphaRAR.attainableSet} is the \emph{closure} of the range of
$\hat{\theta}_{\cdot,k}$ over all times and outcomes; being closed it already contains every a.s.\
limit $z_k$ — in particular $\theta_k$ on the infinitely-sampled event — so the explicit union with
$\{\theta_k\}$ is unnecessary.)
nodes.name: Attainable parameter values
nodes.label: def:attainable

nodes.name: Condition B: regular non-sparse target
nodes.statement_short: Domain open containing attainable values, target twice differentiable with interior values.
nodes.label: def:condB

nodes.statement:
A target function $\Target$ is \emph{sparse at $\Params$} if some component of
$v = \Target(\Params)$ is zero.
nodes.name: Sparse target allocation
nodes.label: def:sparse

nodes.statement:
Let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ be positive reals and $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ random variables.
\begin{itemize}
  \item $X_n = o_p(a_n)$ if for all $\varepsilon > 0$,
        $\Prob\!\big(|X_n|/a_n > \varepsilon\big) \to 0$.
  \item $X_n = O_p(a_n)$ if for all $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $M > 0$ with
        $\limsup_n \Prob\!\big(|X_n|/a_n > M\big) \le \varepsilon$
        (boundedness in probability of $X_n / a_n$).
\end{itemize}
nodes.name: $o_p$ and $O_p$
nodes.label: def:op_Op

nodes.statement:
If $X_n = o_p(a_n)$ and $b_n / a_n \to c \in \R$, then $X_n = o_p(b_n)$
whenever $c \neq 0$; similarly for $O_p$. Moreover $o_p(a_n) + o_p(a_n) = o_p(a_n)$,
$O_p(a_n) + O_p(a_n) = O_p(a_n)$, and $o_p(a_n) + O_p(a_n) = O_p(a_n)$.
nodes.name: $o_p$ and $O_p$ under scaling
nodes.label: lem:op_smul

nodes.statement: Direct from the definitions and a union bound.
nodes.name: Proof of $o_p$ and $O_p$ under scaling
nodes.statement_short: Direct from the definitions and a union bound.

nodes.statement:
Let $K \ge 2$, $\alpha \in [0,1)$ and $m_0 \in \N$ (a burn-in parameter).
A RAR procedure is an \emph{$\alpha$-Rebalancing Targeting Strategy} ($\aRTS$)
if its allocation probabilities $p_{m+1} \in \simplex_K$ satisfy, for all
$m \ge K m_0$, the \emph{throttling condition}
\begin{equation} \forall k \in [K], \quad
  \frac{N_{m,k}}{m} > \hat{\rho}_{m,k}
  \ \Longrightarrow\
  p_{m+1,k} \le \alpha\, \hat{\rho}_{m,k}.
\end{equation}
In words: whenever arm $k$ is currently over-sampled relative to its estimated
target, the probability of selecting it next is throttled down to at most
$\alpha \hat{\rho}_{m,k}$.
nodes.name: $\aRTS$ family
nodes.statement_short: aRTS family: an over-sampled arm's selection probability is throttled to at most alpha times its plug-in target.
nodes.label: def:aRTS

nodes.statement:
\forall k \in [K], \quad
  \frac{N_{m,k}}{m} > \hat{\rho}_{m,k}
  \ \Longrightarrow\
  p_{m+1,k} \le \alpha\, \hat{\rho}_{m,k}.
nodes.name: Throttling condition
nodes.label: eq:throttle

nodes.statement:
The burn-in parameter $m_0$ is the number of initial samples of each arm that
may be taken before adaptive randomization starts. It plays no role in the
proofs; one may take $m_0 = 0$ when the regularization $\theta_0$ of the
estimator is chosen appropriately.
nodes.name: Burn-in parameter plays no role
nodes.label: rem:burnin

nodes.statement:
Given $\alpha \in [0,1)$, the \emph{distance-based} design sets, for
$m \ge K m_0$ and $k \in [K]$,
\[
  p_{m+1,k} = \alpha\, \hat{\rho}_{m,k}
  + (1-\alpha)\frac{\delta_{m,k}}{\sum_{i=1}^K \delta_{m,i}},
  \qquad
  \delta_{m,k} := \max\!\Big(0,\ \hat{\rho}_{m,k} - \frac{N_{m,k}}{m}\Big),
\]
with the convention that if $\delta_{m,j} = 0$ for all $j$, then
$p_{m+1,j} = \hat{\rho}_{m,j}$ for all $j$.
nodes.name: Distance-based design
nodes.statement_short: Mix alpha times the plug-in target with normalized positive deficits.
nodes.label: def:distance_design

nodes.statement:
For all $m \ge K m_0$, the vector $p_{m+1}$ of Definition~\ref{def:distance_design}
lies in $\simplex_K$.
nodes.name: Distance-based is a valid probability vector
nodes.label: lem:distance_simplex

nodes.statement:
Each coordinate is nonnegative, and
$\sum_k p_{m+1,k} = \alpha \sum_k \hat{\rho}_{m,k}
 + (1-\alpha)\frac{\sum_k \delta_{m,k}}{\sum_i \delta_{m,i}} = \alpha + (1-\alpha) = 1$
when some $\delta_{m,i}>0$; in the degenerate case $p_{m+1}=\estTarget_m \in \simplex_K$.
nodes.name: Proof of Distance-based is a valid probability vector
nodes.statement_short: Check nonnegativity and that coordinates sum to one, with the degenerate case separately.

nodes.statement:
The distance-based design satisfies the throttling condition \eqref{eq:throttle},
hence belongs to the $\aRTS$ family.
nodes.name: Distance-based is $\aRTS$
nodes.label: lem:distance_isARTS

nodes.statement:
Membership in $\simplex_K$ is Lemma~\ref{lem:distance_simplex}. For the throttle:
if $N_{m,k}/m > \hat{\rho}_{m,k}$ then $\delta_{m,k} = 0$, so
$p_{m+1,k} = \alpha\hat{\rho}_{m,k} \le \alpha \hat{\rho}_{m,k}$.

\emph{Formalization.} The design is \texttt{AlphaRAR.distanceProb} (a probability-vector function of
the history) and the algorithm \texttt{AlphaRAR.distanceAlgorithm}; \texttt{AlphaRAR.distanceProb\_
throttle} is the throttle inequality. The only subtlety is that the mixing normaliser $\sum_i
\delta_{m,i}$ is positive whenever some arm is over-sampled: the signed deficits
$N_{m,i}/m - \hat\rho_{m,i}$ sum to $0$ (\texttt{sum\_histProp}, \texttt{sum\_histTarget}), so an
over-sampled arm forces an under-sampled one, giving $\delta_{m,j}>0$ for some $j$.
nodes.name: Proof of Distance-based is $\aRTS$
nodes.statement_short: An over-sampled arm has zero deficit, so it only gets alpha times its target.

nodes.statement:
Given $\alpha \in [0,1)$, the \emph{ERADE 2025} design of
\cite{alkhnefr2025efficient} sets, for $m \ge K m_0$ and $k \in [K]$,
\[
  p_{m+1,k} =
  \begin{cases}
    \alpha \hat{\rho}_{m,k}, & N_{m,k}/m > \hat{\rho}_{m,k},\\
    \hat{\rho}_{m,k}, & N_{m,k}/m = \hat{\rho}_{m,k},\\
    \hat{\rho}_{m,k} + (1-\alpha)\dfrac{\sum_{j\in S}\hat{\rho}_{m,j}}{|T|},
      & N_{m,k}/m < \hat{\rho}_{m,k},
  \end{cases}
\]
where $S = \{ j : N_{m,j}/m > \hat{\rho}_{m,j}\}$ is the set of over-sampled arms
and $T = \{ j : N_{m,j}/m < \hat{\rho}_{m,j}\}$ the set of under-sampled arms.
nodes.name: ERADE 2025 design
nodes.statement_short: ERADE: throttle over-sampled arms to alpha times target and redistribute freed mass to under-sampled arms.
nodes.label: def:erade2025

nodes.statement:
For all $m \ge K m_0$, the vector $p_{m+1}$ of Definition~\ref{def:erade2025}
lies in $\simplex_K$.
nodes.name: ERADE 2025 is a valid probability vector
nodes.label: lem:erade2025_simplex

nodes.statement:
Nonnegativity is clear. For the sum, the total mass removed from over-sampled
arms is $\sum_{j\in S}(1-\alpha)\hat{\rho}_{m,j}$, which is exactly the mass
added on the $|T|$ under-sampled arms, and arms with equality keep their target;
using $\sum_k \hat{\rho}_{m,k} = 1$ gives $\sum_k p_{m+1,k} = 1$.
nodes.name: Proof of ERADE 2025 is a valid probability vector
nodes.statement_short: Mass removed from over-sampled arms equals mass added to under-sampled arms.

nodes.statement:
The ERADE 2025 design satisfies \eqref{eq:throttle}, hence belongs to the
$\aRTS$ family.
nodes.name: ERADE 2025 is $\aRTS$
nodes.label: lem:erade2025_isARTS

nodes.statement:
Membership in $\simplex_K$ is Lemma~\ref{lem:erade2025_simplex}. For the throttle:
if $N_{m,k}/m > \hat{\rho}_{m,k}$ then $p_{m+1,k} = \alpha\hat{\rho}_{m,k}$.

\emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.eradeProb}/\texttt{eradeAlgorithm} and
\texttt{AlphaRAR.eradeProb\_throttle}. The simplex identity uses that the mass freed from the
over-sampled arms, $\sum_{j\in S}(1-\alpha)\hat\rho_{m,j}$, is redistributed exactly over the $|T|$
under-sampled arms; the degenerate case $|T|=0$ forces $S=\varnothing$ by mass conservation
(\texttt{sum\_histProp\_le}, \texttt{sum\_histTarget}) --- the proportions never total more than
$1$, which also covers the empty history, where every count is $0$.
nodes.name: Proof of ERADE 2025 is $\aRTS$
nodes.statement_short: Over-sampled arms receive exactly alpha times their target by definition.

nodes.statement:
For $\alpha \in [0,1)$, the \emph{Interpolated D-Tracking} rule sets, for
$m \ge K m_0$ and $k \in [K]$,
\[
  p_{m+1,k} = \alpha\, \hat{\rho}_{m,k} + (1-\alpha)\,\indic_{\{k = k^\star\}},
  \qquad
  k^\star \in \argmax_{a \in [K]} \big\{ m\hat{\rho}_{m,a} - N_{m,a} \big\}.
\]
The quantity $m\hat{\rho}_{m,a} - N_{m,a}$ is the deficit of arm $a$ relative to
its target, so $k^\star$ is the most under-sampled arm.
nodes.name: Interpolated D-Tracking
nodes.statement_short: Mix alpha times the plug-in target with a point mass on the most under-sampled arm.
nodes.label: def:d_tracking

nodes.statement: For all $m \ge K m_0$, $p_{m+1} \in \simplex_K$.
nodes.name: Interpolated D-Tracking is a valid probability vector
nodes.label: lem:d_tracking_simplex

nodes.statement:
$\sum_k p_{m+1,k} = \alpha \sum_k \hat{\rho}_{m,k} + (1-\alpha) = 1$, and each
coordinate is nonnegative.
nodes.name: Proof of Interpolated D-Tracking is a valid probability vector
nodes.statement_short: Coordinates are nonnegative and sum to alpha + (1 - alpha) = 1.

nodes.statement:
For every $\alpha \in [0,1)$, the Interpolated D-Tracking rule satisfies
\eqref{eq:throttle}, hence belongs to the $\aRTS$ family.
nodes.name: Interpolated D-Tracking is $\aRTS$
nodes.label: lem:d_tracking_isARTS

nodes.statement:
Membership in $\simplex_K$ is Lemma~\ref{lem:d_tracking_simplex}.
If $N_{m,k}/m > \hat{\rho}_{m,k}$ then $m\hat{\rho}_{m,k} - N_{m,k} < 0$. Since
$\sum_a (m\hat{\rho}_{m,a} - N_{m,a}) = 0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:counts_sum}, the
maximizing deficit is $\ge 0$, so $k \ne k^\star$ and
$p_{m+1,k} = \alpha\hat{\rho}_{m,k}$.

\emph{Formalization.} The favoured arm $k^\star=\arg\max_a(m\hat\rho_{m,a}-N_{m,a})$ is
\texttt{argmax} of \texttt{AlphaRAR.dtDeficit} (LeanMachineLearning's measurable finite-tuple
\texttt{argmax}, so the policy kernel is measurable without needing an order on the arms); the
throttle is \texttt{AlphaRAR.dTrackingProb\_throttle}.
nodes.name: Proof of Interpolated D-Tracking is $\aRTS$
nodes.statement_short: An over-sampled arm has negative deficit while the max deficit is nonnegative, so it is not the favoured arm.

nodes.statement:
When $\alpha = 0$, the Interpolated D-Tracking rule becomes
$p_{m+1,k} = \indic_{\{k = k^\star\}}$, which is the D-Tracking rule of
\cite{garivier2016optimal} (without its forced-exploration component, treated in
Chapter~\ref{chap:forced}).
nodes.name: D-Tracking as the case alpha = 0
nodes.label: rem:d_tracking_zero

nodes.statement:
For $k \in [K]$ and $m \ge 1$,
\[
  p_{m,k} := \E[X_{m,k} \mid \filt_{m-1}].
\]
For a RAR procedure these coincide with the allocation probabilities: with the
indexing convention of Definition~\ref{def:rar}, $p_{m,k}$ is the $k$-th
component of the vector used to draw $X_m$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Conditional probabilities and the assignment martingale
nodes.name: Conditional selection probability
nodes.label: def:cond_prob

nodes.statement:
$p_{m,k}$ is a \emph{version} of $\E[X_{m,k}\mid\filt_{m-1}]$: it is $\filt_{m-1}$-measurable,
locally integrable, and has the same integral as $X_{m,k}$ over every $\filt_{m-1}$-measurable set
of finite measure. Anything with those three properties is a.s.\ equal to it. The content is the
index: conditioning on $\filt_m$ instead would return $X_{m,k}$ itself, the assignment being known
by then, and $p_{m,k}$ would cease to be a probability of anything.
nodes.section: 3.1 Conditional probabilities and the assignment martingale
nodes.name: $p_{m,k}$ is the conditional probability
nodes.label: lem:cond_prob_unique

nodes.statement:
Existence and a.s.\ uniqueness of the conditional expectation, the latter being the fact that a
$\filt_{m-1}$-measurable function is determined a.s.\ by its integrals over $\filt_{m-1}$-sets.
nodes.section: 3.1 Conditional probabilities and the assignment martingale
nodes.name: Proof of $p_{m,k}$ is the conditional probability
nodes.statement_short: Existence and a.s. uniqueness of conditional expectation.

nodes.statement:
For $k \in [K]$ set $\Delta M_{m,k} := X_{m,k} - p_{m,k}$ and
\[
  M_{n,k} := \sum_{m=1}^n (X_{m,k} - p_{m,k}), \qquad M_n := (M_{n,1},\dots,M_{n,K}).
\]
nodes.section: 3.1 Conditional probabilities and the assignment martingale
nodes.name: Assignment martingale
nodes.label: def:M

nodes.statement:
For each $k \in [K]$, $(M_{n,k})_{n\ge0}$ is an $(\filt_n)$-martingale with
$M_{0,k}=0$ and bounded increments $|\Delta M_{m,k}| \le 1$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Conditional probabilities and the assignment martingale
nodes.name: $M$ is a martingale
conclusions: $(M_{n,k})_{n\ge0}$ is an $(\filt_n)$-martingale with $M_{0,k}=0$ and bounded increments $|\Delta M_{m,k}| \le 1$
nodes.label: lem:M_martingale

nodes.statement:
$\E[\Delta M_{m,k}\mid\filt_{m-1}] = \E[X_{m,k}\mid\filt_{m-1}] - p_{m,k} = 0$
by Definition~\ref{def:cond_prob}, and $X_{m,k},p_{m,k}\in[0,1]$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Conditional probabilities and the assignment martingale
nodes.name: Proof of $M$ is a martingale
nodes.statement_short: Conditional expectation of the increment vanishes by definition of p; increments lie in [-1,1].

nodes.statement:
$M_{\cdot,k}$ is the Doob martingale part of the count $N_{\cdot,k}$ against $(\filt_{n-1})$: it is
an $(\filt_{n-1})$-martingale, $M_{0,k}=0$, and what it removes from the count — the accumulated
selection probabilities $N_{\cdot,k}-M_{\cdot,k}$ — is predictable. Any process with those three
properties is indistinguishable from it. Predictability is what makes the martingale property pin
$M$ down: without it, adding any martingale null at $0$ would give another candidate.
nodes.section: 3.1 Conditional probabilities and the assignment martingale
nodes.name: $M$ is the unique compensator of the count
nodes.label: lem:M_unique

nodes.statement:
Existence is Lemma~\ref{lem:M_martingale} together with predictability of the Doob predictable
part. For uniqueness, $N = M + (N-M)$ exhibits the count as a martingale plus a predictable process
null at $0$, and that decomposition is unique up to null sets, one per time; the index set is
countable, so the exceptional sets union to a null set.
nodes.section: 3.1 Conditional probabilities and the assignment martingale
nodes.name: Proof of $M$ is the unique compensator of the count
nodes.statement_short: Doob decomposition: existence from the martingale property, uniqueness up to countably many null sets.

nodes.statement: For each $k \in [K]$, $M_{n,k} = O_p(\sqrt n)$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Conditional probabilities and the assignment martingale
nodes.name: The assignment martingale is $O_p(\sqrt n)$
nodes.label: lem:M_Op

nodes.statement:
$M_{\cdot,k}$ is a martingale with $M_{0,k}=0$ and increments bounded by $1$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:M_martingale}), so Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_bdd_incr_Op} applies with
$c = 1$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Conditional probabilities and the assignment martingale
nodes.name: Proof of The assignment martingale is $O_p(\sqrt n)$
nodes.statement_short: Apply the bounded-increment O_p lemma with c = 1.

nodes.statement:
For all $n\ge1$ and $k\in[K]$,
$\displaystyle N_{n,k} = \sum_{m=1}^n p_{m,k} + M_{n,k}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Conditional probabilities and the assignment martingale
nodes.name: Count decomposition
nodes.label: lem:count_decomp

nodes.statement: Sum the identity $X_{m,k} = p_{m,k} + \Delta M_{m,k}$ over $m \le n$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Conditional probabilities and the assignment martingale
nodes.name: Proof of Count decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Sum X = p + Delta M over m <= n.

nodes.statement:
For $k \in [K]$ set $Y_{m,k} := \xi_{m,k} - \theta_k$ and
\[
  Q_{n,k} := \sum_{m=1}^n X_{m,k}\,(\xi_{m,k} - \theta_k)
           = \sum_{m=1}^n X_{m,k}\,Y_{m,k},
  \qquad Q_n := (Q_{n,1}, \dots, Q_{n,K}).
\]
nodes.name: Centered response martingale
nodes.label: def:Q

nodes.statement:
For each $k \in [K]$, if the responses are integrable then $(Q_{n,k})_{n\ge0}$ is a
$(\mathcal{G}_n)$-martingale, where $\mathcal{G}_n := \filt_{n-1}\vee\sigma(A_n)$ is the
action-augmented filtration (\texttt{filtrationAction}); a fortiori it is an
$(\filt_n)$-martingale.
nodes.name: $Q$ is a martingale
nodes.label: lem:Q_martingale

nodes.statement:
Write $\Delta Q_{n,k} = X_{n,k}(\xi_{n,k} - \theta_k)$, where $X_{n,k}$ is the
indicator that the assignment $A_n$ equals arm $k$. The natural filtration is the
\emph{action-augmented} one $\mathcal{G}_n = \filt_{n-1}\vee\sigma(A_n)$
(\texttt{filtrationAction}): the assignment $X_{n,k}$ is $\mathcal{G}_n$-measurable
(the arm is known) while the response $\xi_{n,k}$ is not (it is revealed afterwards).
Conditioning on $\mathcal{G}_n$, the response is drawn from the arm's reward kernel
independently of the past given the arm, so its conditional mean is $\theta_k$;
pulling out the $\mathcal{G}_n$-measurable factor $X_{n,k}$ gives
$\E[\Delta Q_{n,k}\mid\mathcal{G}_n] = X_{n,k}(\theta_k-\theta_k)=0$, so $Q_{\cdot,k}$ is
a $\mathcal{G}$-martingale. Since $Q_{n,k}$ is $\filt_{n-1}\subseteq\mathcal{G}_n$-measurable,
the tower property also gives $\E[\Delta Q_{n,k}\mid\filt_{n-1}] = 0$, the paper's
$\filt$-martingale statement.

This is formalized in the \texttt{LeanMachineLearning} algorithm--environment
framework: the arm is the action and the response is the feedback of a stationary
environment with per-arm reward kernel $\nu$, and $\theta_k = \int x\,\nu_k(dx)$ is
the kernel mean. The conditional-mean computation is \texttt{condExp\_feedback}
(which handles the first patient and the general step via the two conditional-distribution
fields of the framework), and the filtration $\mathcal{G}$ is \texttt{filtrationAction}.
nodes.name: Proof of $Q$ is a martingale
nodes.statement_short: Condition on the action-augmented filtration: response mean is theta_k given the arm, so the increment has zero conditional mean.

nodes.statement:
For each $k \in [K]$, conditioning on the action-augmented $\sigma$-algebra
$\mathcal{G}_n = \filt_{n-1}\vee\sigma(A_n)$ (\texttt{filtrationAction}),
\[
  \E\big[(\Delta Q_{n,k})^2 \mid \mathcal{G}_n\big] = X_{n,k}\, V_k,
\]
where $V_k = \Var[\xi_{1,k}] = \int (x-\theta_k)^2\,\nu_k(dx)$ is the variance of arm $k$
(Mathlib's \texttt{variance}: \texttt{Var[id; ν k]}).
nodes.name: Conditional second moment of $\Delta Q$
nodes.label: lem:Q_cond_second_moment

nodes.statement:
Since $X_{n,k}$ is a $\{0,1\}$-indicator, $X_{n,k}^2 = X_{n,k}$ and hence
$(\Delta Q_{n,k})^2 = X_{n,k}(\xi_{n,k}-\theta_k)^2$. The factor $X_{n,k}$ is
$\mathcal{G}_n$-measurable, so it pulls out of the conditional expectation; by the same
conditional-distribution computation as in Lemma~\ref{lem:Q_martingale} --- now applied to
$g(x) = (x-\theta_k)^2$ (\texttt{condExp\_feedback\_comp}) --- the response's conditional
second central moment given $\mathcal{G}_n$ is $\int (x-\theta_k)^2\,\nu_{A_n}(dx)$. On the
event $\{A_n = k\}$ this integral equals $V_k$, while off it $X_{n,k}=0$; in either case
the product is $X_{n,k} V_k$.
nodes.name: Proof of Conditional second moment of $\Delta Q$
nodes.statement_short: Indicator squared is itself; pull it out and compute the conditional second central moment of the response.

nodes.statement:
Under Condition~\textbf{A}, the predictable quadratic variation of $Q_{\cdot,k}$ is
$\langle Q_{\cdot,k}\rangle_n = V_k N_{n,k}$: the process $Q_{\cdot,k}^2 - V_k N_{\cdot,k}$ is a
martingale, with $V_k N_{\cdot,k}$ its predictable compensator.
nodes.name: Quadratic variation of $Q$
nodes.label: lem:Q_quad_var

nodes.statement:
Since $Q_{\cdot,k}$ is a martingale for the action-augmented filtration
$\mathcal{G} = \texttt{filtrationAction}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:Q_martingale}), the paper's
$V_k N_{n,k}$ is the \emph{ordinary} predictable quadratic variation of $Q_{\cdot,k}$ for
$\mathcal{G}$ (Definition~\ref{def:pred_qv}): its increment is
$\E[(\Delta Q_{m+1,k})^2\mid\mathcal{G}_m] = V_k X_{m,k}$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:Q_cond_second_moment}), and summing over $m<n$ gives
$V_k\sum_{m<n} X_{m,k} = V_k N_{n,k}$ --- the indicator survives the sum because the current
arm $A_m$ is $\mathcal{G}_m$-measurable. That $Q^2-\langle Q\rangle$ is a martingale (for
$\mathcal{G}$) is Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_mart}. The sole hypothesis is finite arm variance
(Condition~\textbf{A}), formalized as $\xi_{\cdot,k}\in L^2$.
nodes.name: Proof of Quadratic variation of $Q$
nodes.statement_short: Compute the compensator increment from the conditional second moment and sum.

nodes.statement:
Under Condition~\textbf{A}, for each $k \in [K]$,
$\E[Q_{n,k}^2] = V_k\,\E[N_{n,k}]$.
nodes.name: Second moment of $Q$
nodes.label: lem:Q_second_moment

nodes.statement:
The discrete Itô isometry (Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_second_moment}) gives
$\E[Q_{n,k}^2] = \E[\langle Q_{\cdot,k}\rangle_n]$ for the martingale $Q_{\cdot,k}$ (which starts at
$0$), and $\langle Q_{\cdot,k}\rangle_n = V_k N_{n,k}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:Q_quad_var}; taking
expectations, $\E[Q_{n,k}^2] = V_k\,\E[N_{n,k}]$.
nodes.name: Proof of Second moment of $Q$
nodes.statement_short: Discrete Ito isometry combined with the quadratic variation of Q.

nodes.statement:
For $k \ne j$, the cross variation vanishes: $\langle Q_{\cdot,k}, Q_{\cdot,j}\rangle_n = 0$.
Equivalently, $Q_{\cdot,k}\,Q_{\cdot,j}$ is a martingale (for the action-augmented filtration
$\mathcal{G}$).
nodes.name: Cross variation of $Q$
nodes.label: lem:Q_cross_var

nodes.statement:
The increments $\Delta Q_{\cdot,k}$ and $\Delta Q_{\cdot,j}$ are orthogonal --- indeed their
product is \emph{identically} zero, since $X_{m,k}X_{m,j} = 0$ for $k \ne j$ (each patient is
assigned to exactly one arm, \texttt{respMart\_increment\_mul\_eq\_zero}). Hence
$Q_{\cdot,k}\,Q_{\cdot,j}$ is a martingale by Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_orthogonal}
(\texttt{martingale\_mul}), so its predictable compensator --- the cross variation --- is $0$.
nodes.name: Proof of Cross variation of $Q$
nodes.statement_short: Increments of different arms multiply to zero, so the product is a martingale.

nodes.statement:
For each $k \in [K]$, if the responses are square-integrable (Condition~\textbf{A}), then
$Q_{n,k} = O_p(\sqrt n)$.
nodes.name: The response martingale is $O_p(\sqrt n)$
nodes.label: lem:Q_Op

nodes.statement:
$Q_{\cdot,k}$ is a martingale (for the action-augmented filtration $\mathcal{G}$) with
$Q_{0,k}=0$, and its increment second moments are bounded by the arm variance: taking
expectations in Lemma~\ref{lem:Q_cond_second_moment} via the tower property,
$\E[(\Delta Q_{n+1,k})^2] = \E[X_{n,k}\,V_k] = V_k\,\Prob(X_{n,k}=1) \le V_k$
(\texttt{integral\_respMart\_increment\_sq\_le}). So Corollary~\ref{cor:mart_Op} applies with
$\sigma^2 = V_k$.
nodes.name: Proof of The response martingale is $O_p(\sqrt n)$
nodes.statement_short: Bound the increment second moments by V_k and apply the martingale O_p corollary.

nodes.statement:
On $\{N_{m,k}\ge1\}$, the leading term of the estimator error is
$\dfrac{1}{N_{m,k}}\sum_{j=1}^m X_{j,k}\xi_{j,k} - \theta_k
 = \dfrac{Q_{m,k}}{N_{m,k}}$.
Consequently, under the Bahadur representation
(Definition~\ref{def:bahadur}),
$\hat{\theta}_{m,k} - \theta_k = \dfrac{Q_{m,k}}{N_{m,k}} + o(N_{m,k}^{-1/2})$.
nodes.name: Estimator error via $Q$
nodes.label: lem:theta_error_Q

nodes.statement:
$\frac{1}{N_{m,k}}\sum_j X_{j,k}\xi_{j,k} - \theta_k
= \frac{1}{N_{m,k}}\sum_j X_{j,k}(\xi_{j,k}-\theta_k)
= \frac{Q_{m,k}}{N_{m,k}}$, using $\sum_j X_{j,k} = N_{m,k}$.
nodes.name: Proof of Estimator error via $Q$
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite using the count identity.

nodes.statement:
For a fixed $\alpha \in [0,1)$, $k \in [K]$ and $n \ge 0$ (with the $0$-indexed convention,
patient $0$ first),
\[
  U_{n,k} := \sum_{m=0}^{n-1} \alpha\, \hat{\rho}_{m,k} + M_{n,k} - n\, \hat{\rho}_{n,k}.
\]
The leading sum runs over $m < n$, so it uses the plug-in targets of patients $0,\dots,n-1$.
nodes.section: 3.3 The auxiliary process $U$ and the last hitting time
nodes.name: Auxiliary process $U$
nodes.statement_short: Auxiliary process combining throttled plug-in targets, the assignment martingale and the scaled current target.
nodes.label: def:U

nodes.statement:
For all $n \ge 0$ and $k \in [K]$,
\[
  \Delta U_{n,k} = U_{n+1,k} - U_{n,k}
  = \alpha\, \hat{\rho}_{n,k} - p_{n,k} + \Delta\big(N_{n,k} - n\hat{\rho}_{n,k}\big),
\]
where we used $\Delta M_{n,k} = X_{n,k} - p_{n,k}$ and $\Delta N_{n,k} = X_{n,k}$. The selection
probability $p_{n,k}$ is paired with the target $\hat\rho_{n,k}$ at the \emph{same} index, so the
throttle discharged downstream is $p_{n,k} \le \alpha\hat\rho_{n,k}$ (patient $n$ is allocated using
the target of patients $0,\dots,n-1$). The identity holds at $n=0$ too, since the $\alpha\hat\rho$
sum grows at every step.
nodes.section: 3.3 The auxiliary process $U$ and the last hitting time
nodes.name: Increment of $U$
nodes.label: lem:U_increment

nodes.statement:
Direct computation from Definition~\ref{def:U}, expanding
$M_{n+1,k} - M_{n,k} = X_{n,k} - p_{n,k}$ and telescoping.
nodes.section: 3.3 The auxiliary process $U$ and the last hitting time
nodes.name: Proof of Increment of $U$
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation from the definition of U and telescoping.

nodes.statement:
For $k \in [K]$ and $n \ge 1$, the \emph{last under-sampling time} before $n$ is
\[
  \ell_{n,k} := \max\Big\{\, m \le n : \frac{N_{m,k}}{m} \le \hat{\rho}_{m,k} \,\Big\}.
\]
It is the last time up to $n$ at which arm $k$ is under-sampled (its proportion
is at most its estimated target).
nodes.section: 3.3 The auxiliary process $U$ and the last hitting time
nodes.name: Last under-sampling time
nodes.statement_short: Last time up to n at which arm k is under-sampled relative to its plug-in target.
nodes.label: def:hitting

nodes.statement: For each $k$, $(\ell_{n,k})_{n\ge1}$ is non-decreasing and $\ell_{n,k} \le n$.
nodes.section: 3.3 The auxiliary process $U$ and the last hitting time
nodes.name: Basic properties of the hitting time
nodes.label: lem:hitting_basic

nodes.statement:
Immediate from the definition: enlarging $n$ enlarges the set over which the max
is taken, and the max is bounded by $n$.
nodes.section: 3.3 The auxiliary process $U$ and the last hitting time
nodes.name: Proof of Basic properties of the hitting time
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definition of a running maximum.

nodes.statement:
Well-definedness of $\ell_{n,k}$ requires the set
$\{m\le n : N_{m,k}/m \le \hat\rho_{m,k}\}$ to be nonempty; a convenient
convention (used implicitly in the paper) is that it contains a base time such
as the end of the burn-in, or one sets $\ell_{n,k}=0$ when the set is empty.
nodes.section: 3.3 The auxiliary process $U$ and the last hitting time
nodes.name: Empty-set convention for the hitting time
nodes.statement_short: The last under-sampling time is well defined by a base-time or ell = 0 convention when the set is empty.

nodes.statement:
For $m > \ell_{n,k}$ (and $m \le n$), $\frac{N_{m,k}}{m} > \hat{\rho}_{m,k}$;
in particular, for an $\aRTS$ design with $m \ge Km_0$, $p_{m+1,k} \le \alpha\hat{\rho}_{m,k}$.
nodes.section: 3.3 The auxiliary process $U$ and the last hitting time
nodes.name: Sign at the hitting time
nodes.label: lem:hitting_sign

nodes.statement:
By maximality of $\ell_{n,k}$, no $m$ with $\ell_{n,k} < m \le n$ satisfies
$N_{m,k}/m \le \hat{\rho}_{m,k}$. The second statement is the throttling
condition \eqref{eq:throttle}.
nodes.section: 3.3 The auxiliary process $U$ and the last hitting time
nodes.name: Proof of Sign at the hitting time
nodes.statement_short: Maximality of the hitting time and the throttling condition.

nodes.statement:
Three properties characterize $\ell_{n,k}$: it is $\le n$; no $m$ with $\ell_{n,k}<m\le n$ is
under-sampled; and $\ell_{n,k}$ is itself under-sampled unless it is $0$. No other number has all
three. The last clause is the empty-set convention of the Lean remark above, stated rather than
left implicit — it is what gives $\ell_{n,k}$ a value when arm $k$ is never under-sampled up to
$n$, and what keeps that value from being arbitrary.
nodes.section: 3.3 The auxiliary process $U$ and the last hitting time
nodes.name: The hitting time is the last such time
nodes.label: lem:hitting_unique

nodes.statement:
Existence is Lemmas~\ref{lem:hitting_basic} and~\ref{lem:hitting_sign} together with the fact that
the maximum is attained whenever the set is nonempty. For uniqueness, of two candidates the smaller
one's maximality rules the larger one out, which forces the larger to be $0$ and hence not larger
after all.
nodes.section: 3.3 The auxiliary process $U$ and the last hitting time
nodes.name: Proof of The hitting time is the last such time
nodes.statement_short: Existence from the basic properties; uniqueness by comparing two candidates' maximality.

nodes.statement:
Let $(u_n)_{n\ge1}$ be positive reals and $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ real random variables.
If there is $C > 0$ with $\E|X_n| \le C u_n$ for all $n$, then $X_n = O_p(u_n)$.
nodes.name: Bounded expectation gives $O_p$
assumptions: there is $C > 0$ with $\E|X_n| \le C u_n$ for all $n$
nodes.label: lem:expectation_to_O

nodes.statement:
By Markov's inequality, $\Prob(|X_n| > M u_n) \le \E|X_n|/(M u_n) \le C/M$.
Given $\varepsilon > 0$, take $M \ge C/\varepsilon$ to get
$\Prob(|X_n| > M u_n) \le \varepsilon$ for all $n$, which is the definition of
$X_n = O_p(u_n)$.
nodes.name: Proof of Bounded expectation gives $O_p$
nodes.statement_short: Markov's inequality with M chosen large.

nodes.statement:
Let $(u_n)_{n\ge1}$ be positive reals and $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ real random variables.
If there is $C \ge 0$ with $\E[X_n^2] \le C u_n^2$ for all $n$, then $X_n = O_p(u_n)$.
nodes.name: Bounded second moment gives $O_p$
assumptions: there is $C \ge 0$ with $\E[X_n^2] \le C u_n^2$ for all $n$
nodes.label: lem:sq_expectation_to_O

nodes.statement:
By Chebyshev's inequality, $\Prob(|X_n| > M u_n) = \Prob(X_n^2 > M^2 u_n^2)
\le \E[X_n^2]/(M^2 u_n^2) \le C/M^2$, which is $\le \varepsilon$ once
$M \ge \sqrt{C/\varepsilon}$. Equivalently, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:expectation_to_O}
to $X_n^2$ with rate $u_n^2$ to get $X_n^2 = O_p(u_n^2)$, then take square roots.
nodes.name: Proof of Bounded second moment gives $O_p$
nodes.statement_short: Chebyshev's inequality.

nodes.statement:
Let $\{M_n, \filt_n\}$ be a martingale with $\E|\Delta M_n|^2 \le C_0$ for all
$n$. Then for any integer $L$,
\[
  \E\Big[\max_{1 \le m \le L} |M_n - M_{n-m}|\Big] \le 4\sqrt{C_0 L}.
\]
nodes.name: Doob $L^2$ maximal bound for martingale differences
nodes.statement_short: Doob L2 bound on the expected maximal martingale increment over a window of length L.
nodes.label: lem:mart_maximal

nodes.statement:
Fix $n$ and set $S_k := M_{n-L+k} - M_{n-L}$ for $0 \le k \le L$, a martingale for
the shifted filtration $\mathcal{G}_k := \filt_{n-L+k}$. First,
$\max_{1\le m\le L}|M_n - M_{n-m}| \le 2\max_{1\le k\le L}|S_k|$ by the triangle
inequality. Since $\{S_k^2\}$ is a submartingale, Doob's maximal inequality gives
$\Prob(\max_k |S_k| \ge x) \le \E[S_L^2]/x^2$. Orthogonality of martingale
increments yields $\E[S_L^2] = \sum_{k=1}^L \E|\Delta M_{n-L+k}|^2 \le L C_0$.
Combining, $\Prob(\max_m |M_n - M_{n-m}| \ge x) \le 4 L C_0 / x^2$, and integrating
the tail,
$\E[\max_m |M_n-M_{n-m}|] \le \int_0^{2\sqrt{LC_0}} 1\,dx
 + 4\int_{2\sqrt{LC_0}}^\infty \frac{LC_0}{x^2}\,dx = 4\sqrt{LC_0}$.

\emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.mart\_maximal} states the equivalent $\int^-$ (lintegral)
bound $\int^- \max_{m\le L}|M_n - M_{n-m}| \le 4\sqrt{C_0 L}$ (the $m=0$ term is $0$, so
$\max_{m\le L}=\max_{1\le m\le L}$), which is the form consumed downstream via
\texttt{isBigOpOne\_of\_lintegral\_le}. The three substantive ingredients are separate reusable
lemmas filling a Mathlib gap: the shifted martingale \texttt{AlphaRAR.martingale\_shift}, Doob's
$L^2$ submartingale \texttt{AlphaRAR.submartingale\_sq}, and the $L^2$ maximal inequality
\texttt{AlphaRAR.lintegral\_sup'\_abs\_le\_two\_mul\_sqrt} (whose analytic core is the tail-to-$L^1$
lemma \texttt{MeasureTheory.lintegral\_le\_two\_mul\_sqrt\_of\_meas\_ge\_le}).
nodes.name: Proof of Doob $L^2$ maximal bound for martingale differences
nodes.statement_short: Shift the martingale, use Doob's L2 maximal inequality and orthogonality of increments, then integrate the tail.

nodes.statement:
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_maximal}, for any $L$ with
$0 < L \le n$,
\[
  \E\Big[\max_{L \le m \le n} \frac{|M_n - M_{n-m}|}{m}\Big] \le 32\sqrt{\frac{C_0}{L}}.
\]
nodes.name: Dyadic maximal bound
nodes.label: lem:mart_maximal_dyadic

nodes.statement:
Split the range $[L,n]$ into dyadic blocks $2^{j-1} \le m < 2^j$. On such a block
$\frac1m \le \frac{2}{2^j}$, so
$\E[\max_{L\le m\le n}\frac{|M_n-M_{n-m}|}{m}]
 \le \sum_{j \ge \log_2 L} \frac{2}{2^j}\, \E[\max_{m<2^j}|M_n-M_{n-m}|]
 \le \sum_{j\ge\log_2 L} \frac{2}{2^j}\, 4\sqrt{C_0 2^j}
 = 8\sqrt{C_0}\sum_{j\ge\log_2 L} 2^{-j/2}$
by Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_maximal}. The geometric sum
$\sum_{j\ge\log_2 L} 2^{-j/2} = (2+\sqrt2)\,2^{-\lceil\log_2 L\rceil/2} \le 4/\sqrt L$
(using $\tfrac1{1-1/\sqrt2} = 2+\sqrt2 \le 4$ and $2^{\lceil\log_2 L\rceil}\ge L$), giving the bound
$32\sqrt{C_0/L}$.

\emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.mart\_maximal\_dyadic} states the equivalent $\int^-$
(lintegral) bound $\int^- \max_{L\le m\le n}\frac{|M_n-M_{n-m}|}{m} \le 32\sqrt{C_0/L}$ (the
constant $32 = 8(2+\sqrt2)$ rounded up, which suffices for the downstream $o_p$; the exact
constant is immaterial). The dyadic index of $m$ is $\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor+1$ (\texttt{Nat.log}),
the per-scale bound is Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_maximal} applied at $L' = \min(2^j-1,n)$, and the
geometric series is bounded via \texttt{geom\_sum\_eq} with ratio $1/\sqrt2 \le 3/4$.
nodes.name: Proof of Dyadic maximal bound
nodes.statement_short: Split the range into dyadic blocks and apply the window maximal bound on each; sum a geometric series.

nodes.statement:
Let $(M_{\cdot,k})_{k\in[K]}$ be a finite family of martingales, each satisfying the hypotheses of
Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_maximal} with the same bound $C_0$. Then, for $L\le n$,
\[
  \E\Big[\max_{m\le L}\|M_n - M_{n-m}\|\Big] \le 4K\sqrt{C_0 L},
\]
and, for $0<L\le n$,
\[
  \E\Big[\max_{L\le m\le n}\frac{\|M_n - M_{n-m}\|}{m}\Big] \le 32K\sqrt{\tfrac{C_0}{L}},
\]
where $\|\cdot\|$ is the Euclidean norm on $\R^K$.
nodes.name: Vector maximal bounds
nodes.label: lem:mart_maximal_pi

nodes.statement:
By the $\ell^2\le\ell^1$ inequality $\|v\| = \sqrt{\sum_k v_k^2}\le\sum_k|v_k|$, the running maximum of
the norm is bounded by $\sum_k$ of the coordinatewise running maxima (maximum of a sum $\le$ sum of
maxima), and each coordinate is controlled by Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_maximal} (resp.\
Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_maximal_dyadic}). Summing the $K$ scalar bounds gives the factor $K$.

\emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.mart\_maximal\_pi} and
\texttt{AlphaRAR.mart\_maximal\_dyadic\_pi} state the $\int^-$ forms with the norm written as
$\sqrt{\sum_k(M_{n,k}-M_{n-m,k})^2}$. The coordinate interchange uses \texttt{Finset.sup'\_le} and
\texttt{Finset.le\_sup'}; the $\ell^2\le\ell^1$ step is \texttt{sum\_sq\_le\_sq\_sum\_of\_nonneg};
integration term-by-term is \texttt{lintegral\_finsetSum}.
nodes.name: Proof of Vector maximal bounds
nodes.statement_short: Bound the Euclidean norm by the l1 norm and apply the scalar bounds coordinatewise.

nodes.statement:
For any sequence $(Q_n)_{n\ge0}$ in a normed space, any $\ell$ with
$0 \le \ell \le n$ and any $1 \le L < n$,
\[
  \|Q_n - Q_\ell\| \le (n - \ell)\max_{L \le m \le n}\frac{\|Q_n - Q_{n-m}\|}{m}
   + \max_{m < L}\|Q_n - Q_{n-m}\|.
\]
nodes.name: Increment control from maximal bounds
nodes.label: lem:increment_control

nodes.statement:
Let $d := n - \ell$. If $d < L$, then $\|Q_n - Q_\ell\| = \|Q_n - Q_{n-d}\| \le
\max_{m<L}\|Q_n-Q_{n-m}\|$. If $d \ge L$, then
$\|Q_n - Q_\ell\| = d\cdot \frac{\|Q_n-Q_{n-d}\|}{d}
 \le (n-\ell)\max_{L\le m\le n}\frac{\|Q_n-Q_{n-m}\|}{m}$.
Taking the larger of the two bounds proves the claim.
nodes.name: Proof of Increment control from maximal bounds
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether the gap n - ell is below or above L.

nodes.statement:
Let $\{X_n\}$ be a square-integrable martingale with $\E[X_1] = 0$. Then for
$\lambda > 0$,
\[
  \Prob\Big(\max_{1\le i\le n} X_i \ge \lambda\Big)
  \le \frac{\Var(X_n)}{\Var(X_n) + \lambda^2}.
\]
nodes.name: Kolmogorov-type inequality for martingales
nodes.label: lem:chebyshev_mart

nodes.statement:
For $\alpha > 0$, $\{\max_k X_k \ge \lambda\} \subseteq
\{\max_k (X_k+\alpha)^2 \ge (\lambda+\alpha)^2\}$. As $\{(X_k+\alpha)^2\}$ is a
submartingale, Doob's inequality gives
$\Prob(\max_k(X_k+\alpha)^2 \ge (\lambda+\alpha)^2)
 \le \frac{\E[(X_n+\alpha)^2]}{(\lambda+\alpha)^2}
 = \frac{\Var(X_n)+\alpha^2}{(\lambda+\alpha)^2}$.
Optimizing at $\alpha = \Var(X_n)/\lambda$ gives
$\frac{\Var(X_n)}{\Var(X_n)+\lambda^2}$.
nodes.name: Proof of Kolmogorov-type inequality for martingales
nodes.statement_short: Shift by alpha, apply Doob's inequality to the submartingale (X + alpha)^2, then optimize alpha.

nodes.statement:
Let $\{X_n\}$ be a square-integrable martingale with $X_0 = 0$ and increment
second moments bounded, $\E[(\Delta X_{n+1})^2] \le \sigma^2$ (in particular
stationary increment variances $\Var(X_n) = n\sigma^2$). Then $X_n = O_p(\sqrt n)$.
nodes.name: Martingale is $O_p(\sqrt n)$
nodes.label: cor:mart_Op

nodes.statement:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_sq_growth}, $\E[X_n^2] \le \sigma^2 n$. Chebyshev's
inequality (Lemma~\ref{lem:sq_expectation_to_O}) with rate $u_n = \sqrt n$ then
gives $X_n = O_p(\sqrt n)$: $\Prob(|X_n| > M\sqrt n) \le \E[X_n^2]/(M^2 n)
\le \sigma^2/M^2 \le \varepsilon$ for $M$ large, uniformly in $n$.
nodes.name: Proof of Martingale is $O_p(\sqrt n)$
nodes.statement_short: Martingale L2 growth plus Chebyshev with rate sqrt(n).

nodes.statement:
Let $M$ be a martingale with $M_0 = 0$ whose increments are bounded,
$|\Delta M_{n+1}| \le c$ a.s.\ for all $n$. Then $M_n = O_p(\sqrt n)$.
nodes.name: Bounded-increment martingale is $O_p(\sqrt n)$
assumptions: $M$ be a martingale with $M_0 = 0$ whose increments are bounded
nodes.label: lem:mart_bdd_incr_Op

nodes.statement:
Bounded increments give square-integrability of $M_n$ (indeed $|M_n| \le cn$ a.s.)
and $\E[(\Delta M_{n+1})^2] \le c^2$, so Corollary~\ref{cor:mart_Op} applies with
$\sigma^2 = c^2\,\Prob(\Omega)$.
nodes.name: Proof of Bounded-increment martingale is $O_p(\sqrt n)$
nodes.statement_short: Bounded increments give the second-moment hypothesis of the martingale O_p corollary.

nodes.statement:
For a regular one-parameter exponential family with density
$f(y\mid\eta) = \exp\{\eta y - A(\eta)\}h(y)$, if the parameter of interest
$\theta_k = A'(\eta_k)$ is the mean parameter and $\xi_{1,k} = Y$, then
$\Var(\xi_{1,k}) = I_k(\theta_k)^{-1}$, where $I_k$ is the Fisher information for
one observation.
nodes.name: Variance equals inverse Fisher information
nodes.label: prop:exp_fam

nodes.statement:
For the natural family, $\E_\eta[Y] = A'(\eta)$ and $\Var_\eta(Y) = A''(\eta)$.
With $\theta_k = A'(\eta_k)$ one has $\Var(\xi_{1,k}) = A''(\eta_k)$. By the
reparameterization formula for Fisher information,
$I_k(\theta_k) = I_{\eta_k}(\eta_k)\big(\frac{d\eta_k}{d\theta_k}\big)^2
 = A''(\eta_k)\big(\frac{1}{A''(\eta_k)}\big)^2 = \frac{1}{A''(\eta_k)}$,
so $\Var(\xi_{1,k}) = I_k(\theta_k)^{-1}$.
nodes.name: Proof of Variance equals inverse Fisher information
nodes.statement_short: Mean and variance of the natural family plus the reparameterization formula for Fisher information.

nodes.statement:
Let $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ be a non-decreasing sequence with $a_n \le n$, let
$\alpha, v \in [0,1]$, and let $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ be real with
$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{X_n}{n} = -\alpha v$. Then for any real sequence
$\varepsilon_n$ with $\limsup_n \varepsilon_n \le 0$,
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\Big(\varepsilon_n + \frac{X_n - X_{a_n}}{n}\Big)^+ = 0.
\]
nodes.name: Positive-part convergence
nodes.statement_short: Positive part of a perturbed normalized increment tends to zero along a monotone time change.
assumptions: $(a_n)_{n\ge1}$ be a non-decreasing sequence with $a_n \le n$
nodes.label: lem:convergence

nodes.statement:
If $(a_n)$ is bounded, it is eventually constant, so $X_{a_n}/n \to 0$ and
$\varepsilon_n + \frac{X_n - X_{a_n}}{n} \to -\alpha v \le 0$, whence the positive
part tends to $0$. If $a_n \to \infty$, then $X_{a_n}/a_n \to -\alpha v$; for
$\varepsilon>0$ and $n$ large, $-\frac{X_{a_n}}{n} \le (\varepsilon + \alpha v)\frac{a_n}{n}
 \le \varepsilon + \alpha v$ (using $a_n \le n$), so
$\varepsilon_n + \frac{X_n - X_{a_n}}{n} \le \varepsilon_n + \frac{X_n}{n} + \varepsilon + \alpha v$.
Since $\frac{X_n}{n} + \alpha v \to 0$ and $\limsup \varepsilon_n \le 0$, the
limsup of the left side is $\le \varepsilon$; as $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary the
positive part tends to $0$.
nodes.name: Proof of Positive-part convergence
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on whether the time change a_n is bounded or diverges.

nodes.name: Generic condition set
nodes.statement_short: Abstract conditions on a time sequence ell (monotone, key inequality via U, smallness at ell) under which the main theorems hold.
nodes.label: def:generic_cond

nodes.name: Generic key inequality
nodes.label: eq:generic_ineq

nodes.statement:
N_{\ell_{n,k},k} - \ell_{n,k}\hat{\rho}_{\ell_{n,k},k} = o(\sqrt n)
          \quad\text{a.s.}
nodes.name: Generic smallness at the hitting time
nodes.label: eq:generic_small

nodes.statement:
Suppose a RAR procedure satisfies the generic conditions with some $\ell$, and
that Conditions~\textbf{A}--\textbf{B} hold. Then the conclusions of the strong
consistency theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:LLN}) and of the asymptotic normality
theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:normality}) hold. (The Lean statement
\texttt{consistency\_of\_generic\_ae} formalizes the strong-consistency direction:
the generic conditions and the plug-in-target limit imply $N_{n,k}/n \to u_k$ a.s.\ for every
arm; the asymptotic-normality direction is not yet formalized.)
nodes.name: Generic conditions imply the main theorems
nodes.statement_short: The generic conditions plus Conditions A-B imply both main theorems.
assumptions: Suppose a RAR procedure satisfies the generic conditions with some $\ell$
nodes.label: thm:generic_main

nodes.statement:
This is the content of Chapters~\ref{chap:consistency} and \ref{chap:normality}:
those chapters derive Theorem~\ref{thm:LLN} and Theorem~\ref{thm:normality}
using only the generic conditions of Definition~\ref{def:generic_cond} (together
with Conditions~\textbf{A}--\textbf{B}), never the specific form of the design.
nodes.name: Proof of Generic conditions imply the main theorems
nodes.statement_short: Pointer to Chapters 6-7, which use only the generic conditions.

nodes.statement:
For any $\aRTS$ design and any $\ell_{n,k} \le n$,
\[
  N_{n,k} - n\hat{\rho}_{n,k}
  = N_{\ell_{n,k},k} - \ell_{n,k}\hat{\rho}_{\ell_{n,k},k}
    + \sum_{m=\ell_{n,k}}^{n-1}\big(p_{m,k} - \alpha\hat{\rho}_{m,k}\big)
    + U_{n,k} - U_{\ell_{n,k},k}.
\]
nodes.name: Telescoping identity for $U$
nodes.statement_short: Telescoping identity linking count-target deviation at n and at ell via U and throttle sums.
nodes.label: lem:U_telescope

nodes.statement:
Summing the increment identity of Lemma~\ref{lem:U_increment} from
$m = \ell_{n,k}$ to $n-1$ gives
$U_{n,k} - U_{\ell_{n,k},k}
 = \sum_{m=\ell_{n,k}}^{n-1} (\alpha\hat{\rho}_{m,k} - p_{m,k})
   + (N_{n,k}-n\hat{\rho}_{n,k}) - (N_{\ell_{n,k},k}-\ell_{n,k}\hat{\rho}_{\ell_{n,k},k})$.
Rearranging yields the claim.
nodes.name: Proof of Telescoping identity for $U$
nodes.statement_short: Sum the U-increment identity and rearrange.

nodes.statement:
For any $\aRTS$ design, inequality \eqref{eq:generic_ineq} holds with the last
under-sampling time of Definition~\ref{def:hitting}:
\[
  N_{n,k} - n\hat{\rho}_{n,k}
  \le 1 + N_{\ell_{n,k},k} - \ell_{n,k}\hat{\rho}_{\ell_{n,k},k}
    + U_{n,k} - U_{\ell_{n,k},k}.
\]
nodes.name: Key inequality for $\aRTS$
nodes.label: lem:preliminary_ineq

nodes.statement:
In Lemma~\ref{lem:U_telescope}, each summand $p_{m,k} - \alpha\hat{\rho}_{m,k}$
with $\ell_{n,k} < m \le n-1$ is $\le 0$: indeed $m > \ell_{n,k}$ so arm $k$
is over-sampled at time $m$ and the throttling condition
(Lemma~\ref{lem:hitting_sign}) gives $p_{m,k} \le \alpha\hat{\rho}_{m,k}$.
Dropping this nonpositive sum and bounding the single leftover boundary term
$p_{\ell_{n,k},k} \le 1$ gives the inequality.
nodes.name: Proof of Key inequality for $\aRTS$
nodes.statement_short: Drop the nonpositive throttled summands after the hitting time and bound the boundary term by 1.

nodes.statement:
For any $\aRTS$ design, \eqref{eq:generic_small} holds:
$N_{\ell_{n,k},k} - \ell_{n,k}\hat{\rho}_{\ell_{n,k},k} \le Km_0 = o(\sqrt n)$.
nodes.name: Smallness at the hitting time for $\aRTS$
nodes.label: lem:preliminary_small

nodes.statement:
If $\ell_{n,k} \ge Km_0+1$, then by definition of the hitting time
$N_{\ell_{n,k},k}/\ell_{n,k} \le \hat{\rho}_{\ell_{n,k},k}$, so the difference is
$\le 0$. If $\ell_{n,k} < Km_0+1$, then $N_{\ell_{n,k},k} \le \ell_{n,k} \le Km_0$,
so the difference is $\le Km_0$. Either way it is bounded by the constant $Km_0$,
which is $o(\sqrt n)$.
nodes.name: Proof of Smallness at the hitting time for $\aRTS$
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether the hitting time exceeds the burn-in.

nodes.statement:
Every $\aRTS$ design satisfies the generic conditions
(Definition~\ref{def:generic_cond}) with $\ell_{n,k}$ the last under-sampling
time of Definition~\ref{def:hitting}.
nodes.name: $\aRTS$ satisfies the generic conditions
nodes.statement_short: Every aRTS design satisfies the generic conditions with the last under-sampling time.
nodes.label: prop:aRTS_generic

nodes.statement:
Condition (i) is Lemma~\ref{lem:hitting_basic}, condition (ii) is
Lemma~\ref{lem:preliminary_ineq}, and condition (iii) is
Lemma~\ref{lem:preliminary_small}. (The Lean lemmas
\texttt{generic\_ineq\_of\_hitting} and \texttt{generic\_small\_of\_hitting} package
Lemmas~\ref{lem:preliminary_ineq}--\ref{lem:preliminary_small} at the last under-sampling time
$\ell_{n,k}$ into the operational forms \eqref{eq:generic_ineq}--\eqref{eq:generic_small},
given the $\aRTS$ throttle $\neg P_m \Rightarrow p_{m}\le\alpha\hat\rho_m$ (patient $m$ throttled
by the target at the same index $m$). A single boundary summand $p_{\ell,k}-\alpha\hat\rho_{\ell,k}$
is uncontrolled by the throttle, so the constant in \eqref{eq:generic_ineq} is $1$. No lower bound
on $\ell_{n,k}$ is needed: the telescoping identity holds at $\ell_{n,k}=0$ as well (the
$\alpha\hat\rho$ sum of $U$ grows at every step), so the $0$-indexed edge case is automatic. The
remaining step is to verify that a concrete $\aRTS$ design's selection probabilities satisfy the
throttle — this is Definition~\ref{def:aRTS_alg} and Corollary~\ref{cor:aRTS_alg_consistency}.)
nodes.name: Proof of $\aRTS$ satisfies the generic conditions
nodes.statement_short: Each generic condition is one of the preceding lemmas.

nodes.statement:
Consider an $\aRTS$ design driven by an algorithm–environment sequence under a stationary
environment, with $Y_n\in L^2$ (Condition~\textbf{A}) and a continuous simplex-valued target map
$\Target$. If the design's selection probabilities satisfy the throttle
$\neg P_{m,k}\Rightarrow p_{m,k}\le\alpha\hat\rho_{m,k}$ a.s., then almost surely there is a common
limit vector $v$ with $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ and $\hat\rho_{n,k}\to v_k$ for every arm $k$.
nodes.name: Strong consistency of the aRTS proportions
nodes.label: cor:aRTS_consistency

nodes.statement:
Instantiate Theorem~\ref{thm:generic_main} with the assignment indicators
$Y_{n,k}=\mathbf 1\{A_n=k\}$, the selection probabilities
$p_{n,k}=P[\mathbf 1\{A_n=k\}\mid\filt_{n-1}]$, the plug-in target
$\hat\rho_{n,k}=\Target(\estParams_n)_k$, and $\ell_{n,k}$ the last under-sampling time. The generic
conditions are discharged by Proposition~\ref{prop:aRTS_generic} (the throttle is the stated design
hypothesis); the vanishing normalized assignment martingale $M_{n,k}/n\to0$ is
Lemma~\ref{lem:M_lln}, and the plug-in-target convergence $\hat\rho_{n,k}\to v_k$ is
Lemma~\ref{lem:rho_converges}. The common limit $v_k$ is that of $\hat\rho_{\cdot,k}$.
nodes.name: Proof of Strong consistency of the aRTS proportions
nodes.statement_short: Instantiate the generic theorem with the aRTS objects and discharge its hypotheses.

nodes.statement:
An algorithm chooses the action of patient $n$ from a history $h$ of the $n$ completed rounds
(patients $0,\dots,n-1$) via a Markov kernel; the probability it assigns to arm $k$ is
$\mathrm{policy}_n(h)(\{k\})$. The algorithm
is an \emph{$\alpha$-throttled $\aRTS$ design} with offsets $\Params_0$ and target map $\Target$ if
its policy throttles every over-sampled arm: for every history $h$ and arm $k$, if
$N_{n,k}(h) > n\,\hat\rho_k(h)$ then $\mathrm{policy}_n(h)(\{k\}) \le \alpha\,\hat\rho_k(h)$,
where the count $N(h)$ and target $\hat\rho(h)=\Target(\estParams(h))$ are computed from $h$.
At $n=0$ the condition is vacuous, since $N_{0,k}=0$.
nodes.section: 5.3 The $\aRTS$ family as a property of an algorithm
nodes.name: $\aRTS$ algorithm
nodes.label: def:aRTS_alg

nodes.statement:
If the driving algorithm is an $\aRTS$ design (Definition~\ref{def:aRTS_alg}), under the hypotheses
of Corollary~\ref{cor:aRTS_consistency}, then almost surely $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ and
$\hat\rho_{n,k}\to v_k$ for every arm $k$. The companion
\texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTS\_pullCount\_div\_ae\_tendsto} restates the proportion limit
$N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ with the pull count $N_{n,k}=\texttt{pullCount}$, the vocabulary in which the
loglog estimator rate (Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_LIL},
\texttt{abs\_estimator\_sub\_le\_rate\_loglog\_of\_proportion}) consumes it; only the strict
positivity $v_k>0$ is then still required to apply that rate.
nodes.section: 5.3 The $\aRTS$ family as a property of an algorithm
nodes.name: Consistency of an $\aRTS$ algorithm
nodes.label: cor:aRTS_alg_consistency

nodes.statement:
The policy-level throttle discharges the process-level throttle hypothesis of
Corollary~\ref{cor:aRTS_consistency}. The link is that the selection probability
$p_{n+1,k}=P[\mathbf 1\{A_{n+1}=k\}\mid\filt_n]$ equals
$\mathrm{policy}_{n+1}(\text{history}_{n+1})(\{k\})$ almost surely — a conditional expectation computed from the algorithm's conditional distribution of
the next action given the history (\texttt{HasCondDistrib.condExp\_comp\_eq}) — and the history-level
count and target agree with the process count $N_{n+1,k}$ and target $\hat\rho_{n+1,k}$.
nodes.section: 5.3 The $\aRTS$ family as a property of an algorithm
nodes.name: Proof of Consistency of an $\aRTS$ algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Policy-level throttle implies the process-level throttle via conditional distributions.

nodes.statement:
Throughout the chapter we fix a RAR procedure satisfying the generic conditions
(Definition~\ref{def:generic_cond}) with some $\ell_{n,k}$, and we assume
Conditions~\textbf{A}--\textbf{B}.
nodes.name: Standing assumptions of Chapters 6-7
also_stated_at:
a RAR
procedure satisfying the generic conditions with some $\ell_{n,k}$, and
Conditions~\textbf{A}--\textbf{B}.

nodes.statement:
For each arm $k$, on the event $\{N_{n,k}\to\infty\}$ the bracket-normalized response
martingale vanishes: $\dfrac{Q_{n,k}}{N_{n,k}}\to 0$ a.s.
nodes.name: SLLN for the response martingale
nodes.label: lem:respMart_div_count_slln

nodes.statement:
The response martingale $Q_{\cdot,k}$ has predictable quadratic variation
$\langle Q_k\rangle_n = V_k N_{n,k}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:Q_quad_var}). If $V_k>0$, then on
$\{N_{n,k}\to\infty\}$ the bracket $\langle Q_k\rangle_n = V_k N_{n,k}\to\infty$, so the
bracket-normalized strong law (Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_slln_bracket}) gives
$Q_{n,k}/\langle Q_k\rangle_n\to0$, whence
$Q_{n,k}/N_{n,k} = V_k\,(Q_{n,k}/\langle Q_k\rangle_n)\to0$. If $V_k=0$, then
$\E[Q_{n,k}^2] = V_k\,\E[N_{n,k}] = 0$, so $Q_{n,k}=0$ a.s.\ for every $n$ and the ratio is
identically $0$.
nodes.name: Proof of SLLN for the response martingale
nodes.statement_short: Bracket-normalized martingale SLLN when V_k > 0; degenerate case V_k = 0 separately.

nodes.statement:
For each arm $k$, on the event $\{N_{n,k}\to\infty\}$ the estimator converges a.s.\ to the arm
mean: $\hat\theta_{n,k}\to\theta_k$.
nodes.name: Estimator limit on $\{N\to\infty\}$
nodes.label: lem:theta_limit_infinite

nodes.statement:
By the exact error identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:estimator_bahadur}),
$\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k = (Q_{n,k}+(\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k))/(N_{n,k}+1)$. On
$\{N_{n,k}\to\infty\}$ the constant offset is $O(N_{n,k}^{-1})\to0$, while
$\frac{Q_{n,k}}{N_{n,k}+1} = \frac{Q_{n,k}}{N_{n,k}}\cdot\frac{N_{n,k}}{N_{n,k}+1}\to0\cdot1=0$
by Lemma~\ref{lem:respMart_div_count_slln}. Hence $\hat\theta_{n,k}\to\theta_k$.
nodes.name: Proof of Estimator limit on $\{N\to\infty\}$
nodes.statement_short: Exact error identity plus the SLLN for the response martingale.

nodes.statement:
For each arm $k$ and each realization, if $N_{n,k}\not\to\infty$ then $\hat\theta_{n,k}$ is
eventually constant, and in particular converges.
nodes.name: Estimator eventually constant on $\{\sup_n N<\infty\}$
conclusions: $\hat\theta_{n,k}$ is eventually constant, and in particular converges
nodes.label: lem:theta_limit_finite

nodes.statement:
The count $N_{\cdot,k}$ is a nondecreasing $\N$-valued sequence, so $N_{n,k}\not\to\infty$
forces it to be bounded, hence eventually constant at its supremum $N_{N_0,k}$. For $n\ge N_0$
no further patient is assigned to arm $k$, so both the numerator $\sum_{j<n}X_{j,k}\xi_{j,k}$
and the denominator $N_{n,k}+1$ of $\hat\theta_{n,k}$ are frozen; hence $\hat\theta_{n,k}$ is
eventually constant.
nodes.name: Proof of Estimator eventually constant on $\{\sup_n N<\infty\}$
nodes.statement_short: A bounded monotone integer count is eventually constant, freezing the estimator.

nodes.statement:
For each arm $k$, the estimator $\hat\theta_{n,k}$ converges a.s.: to $\theta_k$ on
$\{N_{n,k}\to\infty\}$ and to an eventually-attained value on $\{\sup_n N_{n,k}<\infty\}$.
nodes.name: The sequential estimator converges a.s.
nodes.label: lem:theta_converges

nodes.statement:
The alternative $N_{n,k}\to\infty$ versus $\sup_n N_{n,k}<\infty$ is exhaustive (as $N_{n,k}$
is monotone in $n$); branch~1 is Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_limit_infinite} and branch~2 is
Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_limit_finite}.
nodes.name: Proof of The sequential estimator converges a.s.
nodes.statement_short: Exhaustive dichotomy between the two preceding lemmas.

nodes.statement:
Under Condition~\textbf{A}, for each $k$ the estimator $\hat{\theta}_{n,k}$
converges a.s.\ to a limit in $I_k$: on $\{N_{n,k}\to\infty\}$ it converges to
$\theta_k$ by the strong law of large numbers; on $\{\sup_n N_{n,k} < \infty\}$
it is eventually constant and its limit lies in $V_k^{\mathrm{att}}$.
nodes.name: Dichotomy for the estimator limit
nodes.label: lem:theta_limit_dichotomy

nodes.statement:
On $\{N_{n,k}\to\infty\}$, the estimator converges a.s.\ to $\theta_k$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_limit_infinite} (the martingale strong law applied to $Q_{\cdot,k}$). On
$\{\sup_n N_{n,k}<\infty\}$, only finitely many responses on arm $k$ are ever
observed, so $\hat{\theta}_{n,k}$ is eventually constant with a value in
$V_k^{\mathrm{att}}$.

\emph{Formalization} (\texttt{AlphaRAR.estimator\_limit\_mem\_attainableSet}). With the closure form
of $I_k$ (Definition~\ref{def:attainable}) the case split is unnecessary: \emph{any} pointwise limit
of $\hat{\theta}_{\cdot,k}$ is a limit of values in the range of the estimator, hence lies in the
closure of that range, i.e.\ in $I_k$ (Mathlib's \texttt{mem\_closure\_of\_tendsto}).
nodes.name: Proof of Dichotomy for the estimator limit
nodes.statement_short: Two-branch argument; in Lean, closure of the range removes the case split.

nodes.statement:
With finitely many arms, the per-arm a.s.\ limits of Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_converges} combine
into a single a.s.\ limit vector: almost surely there is $z\in\R^K$ with
$\estParams_n = (\hat\theta_{n,1},\dots,\hat\theta_{n,K}) \to z$.
nodes.name: The estimator vector converges a.s.
nodes.label: lem:theta_converges_vec

nodes.statement:
Each component converges a.s.\ by Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_converges}; intersecting the finitely
many almost-sure events and choosing the (unique) limits componentwise gives a single a.s.\
event on which the whole vector converges.
nodes.name: Proof of The estimator vector converges a.s.
nodes.statement_short: Intersect finitely many a.s. events.

nodes.statement:
For any continuous target map $\Target$, the plug-in target $\estTarget_n = \Target(\estParams_n)$
converges a.s.: almost surely there is $u\in\R^K$ with $\hat\rho_{n,k}\to u_k$ for every $k$,
where $u = \Target(z)$ and $z$ is the a.s.\ limit of $\estParams_n$.
nodes.name: Convergence of $\estTarget$ by continuity
nodes.label: lem:rho_converges_cont

nodes.statement:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_converges_vec}, $\estParams_n \to z$ a.s.\ (in the product topology of
$\R^K$). Continuity of $\Target$ transports this to
$\estTarget_n = \Target(\estParams_n) \to \Target(z) =: u$, and taking components gives
$\hat\rho_{n,k}\to u_k$.
nodes.name: Proof of Convergence of $\estTarget$ by continuity
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of the target map transports convergence of the estimator vector.

nodes.statement:
Under Conditions~\textbf{A}--\textbf{B} there is a random $u \in (0,1)^K$ with
$\estTarget_n \to u$ a.s. Concretely $u = \Target(z)$ where $z\in I_1\times\dots\times I_K$
is the a.s.\ limit of $\estParams_n$.
nodes.name: Non-sparse limit of $\estTarget$
conclusions: there is a random $u \in (0,1)^K$ with $\estTarget_n \to u$ a.s.
nodes.label: lem:rho_converges

nodes.statement:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:rho_converges_cont} (with $\Target$ continuous on $\hilb$ by Condition~\textbf{B})
and Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_limit_dichotomy}, $\estParams_n \to z$ a.s.\ with
$z \in I_1\times\dots\times I_K$. By Condition~\textbf{B}, $\Target$ is
continuous on the open set $\hilb \supseteq I_1\times\dots\times I_K$ and maps
$I_1\times\dots\times I_K$ into $(0,1)^K$; hence
$\estTarget_n = \Target(\estParams_n) \to \Target(z) =: u \in (0,1)^K$.

\emph{Formalization} (\texttt{AlphaRAR.rho\_converges\_pos}). Condition~\textbf{B}'s non-sparsity
enters as the hypothesis \texttt{hTpos}: $\Target$ maps the product of the attainable sets
(Definition~\ref{def:attainable}) into the positive orthant. With $z$ the a.s.\ estimator-vector
limit (\texttt{estimator\_ae\_tendsto\_pi}), each $z_k\in I_k$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_limit_dichotomy}), so \texttt{hTpos} gives $u_k=\Target(z)_k>0$ while
continuity of $\Target$ gives $\hat\rho_{n,k}\to u_k$. The formalized conclusion is the positivity
$u_k>0$ (the non-sparsity used downstream in Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_consistent}); the matching upper
bound $u_k<1$ is the immediate consequence of the simplex constraint $\sum_k\Target(z)_k=1$.
nodes.name: Proof of Non-sparse limit of $\estTarget$
nodes.statement_short: Continuity on the open domain containing the attainable set, plus interior values under Condition B.

nodes.statement: $M_{n,k} = o(n)$ a.s.\ for each $k$.
nodes.name: LLN for the assignment martingale
nodes.label: lem:M_lln

nodes.name: Proof of LLN for the assignment martingale
nodes.statement_short: Martingale SLLN for bounded increments.

nodes.statement:
Under Conditions~\textbf{A}--\textbf{B}, for each $k$,
$\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{U_{n,k}}{n} = -(1-\alpha)\,u_k$ a.s.,
where $u$ is the limit from Lemma~\ref{lem:rho_converges}. (The formalized statement
\texttt{auxU\_div\_tendsto} is the deterministic core: for real sequences with $\rho_n\to u$ and
$M_n/n\to0$, one has $U_n/n\to-(1-\alpha)u$; the a.s.\ statement is the pathwise application with the
a.s.\ limits from Lemmas~\ref{lem:M_lln} and~\ref{lem:rho_converges}.)
nodes.name: Limit of $U/n$
nodes.label: lem:U_over_n

nodes.statement:
From Definition~\ref{def:U},
$\frac{U_{n,k}}{n} = \frac{\alpha}{n}\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}\hat{\rho}_{m,k}
 - \hat{\rho}_{n,k} + \frac{M_{n,k}}{n}$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:M_lln} the last term is $o(1)$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:rho_converges}
$\hat{\rho}_{n,k}\to u_k$, and by Cesàro
$\frac1n\sum_{m<n}\hat{\rho}_{m,k}\to u_k$. Hence
$\frac{U_{n,k}}{n} \to \alpha u_k - u_k = -(1-\alpha)u_k$.
nodes.name: Proof of Limit of $U/n$
nodes.statement_short: Expand U/n and use the martingale LLN, convergence of the target and Cesaro.

nodes.statement:
Under the generic conditions and Conditions~\textbf{A}--\textbf{B}, for each $k$,
$\big(\frac{N_{n,k}}{n} - \hat{\rho}_{n,k}\big)^+ \to 0$ a.s. (The formalized statement
\texttt{pos\_part\_vanishes} is the pathwise core: it takes as hypotheses the plug-in convergence
$\rho_n\to u$ (\ref{lem:rho_converges}), the vanishing $M_n/n\to0$ (\ref{lem:M_lln}), and the two
generic conditions \eqref{eq:generic_ineq}--\eqref{eq:generic_small} in operational form.)
nodes.name: Positive part vanishes
nodes.label: lem:pos_part_vanishes

nodes.statement:
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:convergence} with $X_n := U_{n,k}$, $a_n := \ell_{n,k}$
(non-decreasing, $\le n$ by the generic conditions), and
$\varepsilon_n := \frac1n + \frac{N_{\ell_{n,k},k}-\ell_{n,k}\hat{\rho}_{\ell_{n,k},k}}{n}$,
which satisfies $\limsup\varepsilon_n \le 0$ by \eqref{eq:generic_small}. Since
$\frac{U_{n,k}}{n}\to -(1-\alpha)u_k$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:U_over_n}), the lemma yields
$\big(\varepsilon_n + \frac{U_{n,k}-U_{\ell_{n,k},k}}{n}\big)^+ \to 0$. Combined
with the generic inequality \eqref{eq:generic_ineq}, which bounds
$\frac{N_{n,k}}{n}-\hat{\rho}_{n,k}$ by that quantity, we get
$\big(\frac{N_{n,k}}{n}-\hat{\rho}_{n,k}\big)^+\to0$.
nodes.name: Proof of Positive part vanishes
nodes.statement_short: Apply the analytic positive-part convergence lemma to U along the hitting times, then use the generic inequality.

nodes.statement:
Under the same hypotheses, for each $k$,
$\big(\hat{\rho}_{n,k} - \frac{N_{n,k}}{n}\big)^+ \to 0$ a.s.
nodes.name: Negative part vanishes
nodes.label: lem:neg_part_vanishes

nodes.statement:
Using $\sum_j N_{n,j}/n = 1$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:counts_sum}) and
$\sum_j \hat{\rho}_{n,j} = 1$,
$\big(\hat{\rho}_{n,k} - \frac{N_{n,k}}{n}\big)^+
 = \big(\sum_{j\ne k}(\frac{N_{n,j}}{n} - \hat{\rho}_{n,j})\big)^+
 \le \sum_{j\ne k}\big(\frac{N_{n,j}}{n} - \hat{\rho}_{n,j}\big)^+ \to 0$
by Lemma~\ref{lem:pos_part_vanishes}.
nodes.name: Proof of Negative part vanishes
nodes.statement_short: Simplex constraints turn the negative part into a sum of positive parts of the other arms.

nodes.statement:
Under the same hypotheses, for each $k$,
$\frac{N_{n,k}}{n} - \hat{\rho}_{n,k} \to 0$ and
$\frac{N_{n,k}}{n} \to u_k \in (0,1)$ a.s. (The formalized statement \texttt{match\_proportion}
delivers $\frac{N_{n,k}}{n}\to u_k$ from the two vanishing positive parts and $\hat{\rho}_{n,k}\to
u_k$.)
nodes.name: Proportions match the plug-in target
nodes.label: lem:match

nodes.statement:
The absolute value $|\frac{N_{n,k}}{n}-\hat{\rho}_{n,k}|$ is the sum of the two
positive parts, both tending to $0$ by
Lemmas~\ref{lem:pos_part_vanishes}--\ref{lem:neg_part_vanishes}. Since
$\hat{\rho}_{n,k}\to u_k$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:rho_converges}), also
$\frac{N_{n,k}}{n}\to u_k$.
nodes.name: Proof of Proportions match the plug-in target
nodes.statement_short: Absolute gap is the sum of the two vanishing positive parts.

nodes.statement: Under the same hypotheses, $N_{n,k}\to\infty$ a.s.\ for every $k$.
nodes.section: 6.4 Identification of the limit and consistency
nodes.name: All arms sampled infinitely often
nodes.label: lem:all_arms_infinite

nodes.statement:
Since $\frac{N_{n,k}}{n}\to u_k > 0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:match}), $N_{n,k}\sim u_k n
\to\infty$.
nodes.section: 6.4 Identification of the limit and consistency
nodes.name: Proof of All arms sampled infinitely often
nodes.statement_short: Positive limiting proportion forces linear growth.

nodes.statement:
Given the a.s.\ vanishing positive gaps for every arm (Lemma~\ref{lem:pos_part_vanishes}) and the
plug-in-target limits $\hat\rho_{n,k}\to u_k$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:rho_converges_cont}), together with
the simplex constraints ($\sum_k X_{j,k}=1$ and $\sum_k\hat\rho_{n,k}=1$), the proportions converge
a.s.\ to the target: $N_{n,k}/n \to u_k$ for all arms $k$ simultaneously.
nodes.section: 6.4 Identification of the limit and consistency
nodes.name: A.s. consistency of the proportions
nodes.label: lem:consistency_matching

nodes.statement:
For each arm the negative gap vanishes by Lemma~\ref{lem:neg_part_vanishes}, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:match} then yields $N_{n,k}/n\to u_k$; intersecting the finitely many a.s.\ events
over the arms gives the simultaneous statement.
nodes.section: 6.4 Identification of the limit and consistency
nodes.name: Proof of A.s. consistency of the proportions
nodes.statement_short: Combine the vanishing gaps arm by arm and intersect a.s. events.

nodes.statement:
Under the same hypotheses, $\estParams_n \to \Params$ a.s., and consequently
$\hat{\rho}_n \to v = \Target(\Params)$ and $\frac{N_{n,k}}{n}\to v_k$ a.s.
nodes.section: 6.4 Identification of the limit and consistency
nodes.name: Estimator consistency
nodes.label: lem:theta_consistent

nodes.statement:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:all_arms_infinite} every arm is sampled infinitely often, so
the first branch of Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_limit_dichotomy} applies to every $k$:
$\hat{\theta}_{n,k}\to\theta_k$. Continuity of $\Target$ gives
$\hat{\rho}_n\to\Target(\Params)=v$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:match} the limit $u$ of
$N_n/n$ equals $v$.

\emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.theta\_consistent\_pi\_of\_condB} discharges this from the
\emph{joint} consistency (a common a.s.\ limit $u$ with both $N_{n,k}/n\to u_k$ and
$\hat\rho_{n,k}\to u_k$) plus Condition~\textbf{B}: since $\hat\rho_{n,k}=\Target(\estParams_n)_k\to
\Target(z)_k$ ($z$ the estimator-vector limit) the shared limit is $u=\Target(z)$, which
Condition~\textbf{B}'s non-sparsity (\texttt{hTpos}, Lemma~\ref{lem:rho_converges}) makes positive;
positivity gives $N_{n,k}\to\infty$ (\texttt{all\_arms\_infinite}), so the dichotomy's infinite branch
(\texttt{estimator\_ae\_tendsto\_of\_pullCount\_atTop}) identifies each limit as the arm mean. For an
aRTS design the joint consistency is exactly \texttt{aRTS\_consistency\_of\_isARTS} (whose plug-in
target \texttt{aRTSTarget} is by definition $\Target(\estParams_n)$), giving the fully discharged
\texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTS\_theta\_consistent}: $\estParams_n\to\Params$ a.s.\ under only the aRTS design
hypotheses and Condition~\textbf{B}. (\texttt{AlphaRAR.theta\_consistent} is the per-arm core taking
the positive proportion as hypothesis.)
nodes.section: 6.4 Identification of the limit and consistency
nodes.name: Proof of Estimator consistency
nodes.statement_short: All arms infinitely sampled, so the estimator converges to theta; continuity identifies the limit.

nodes.statement:
Under the same hypotheses,
$\estParams_n - \Params = O\!\big(\sqrt{\tfrac{\log\log n}{n}}\big)$ a.s. (the sharp $\log\log$ rate;
a coarser $\log$ form is also formalized). The formalized statement
\texttt{abs\_estimator\_sub\_le\_rate\_loglog\_of\_proportion} assembles the pathwise core: from the
exact error identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:estimator_bahadur}), the two-sided $\log\log$ bound
$|Q_{n,k}|\le C\sqrt{n\log\log n}$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:subsampled_lil}, converted from the pull count
$N_{n,k}$ to the time index $n$ via $N_{n,k}\sim v_k n$) and $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k>0$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:match}), it gives $|\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k|\le C'\,\sqrt{n\log\log n}/n =
C'\sqrt{\log\log n/n}$ for large $n$.
nodes.name: LIL rate for the estimator
nodes.label: lem:theta_LIL

nodes.statement:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:estimator_bahadur} the error is exactly
$\hat{\theta}_{n,k}-\theta_k = (Q_{n,k}+(\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k))/(N_{n,k}+1)$. Optional skipping turns
$Q_{\cdot,k}$ into a predictably subsampled i.i.d.\ partial sum, so the subsampled Hartman--Wintner
LIL (Corollary~\ref{cor:subsampled_lil}) gives $|Q_{n,k}| = O(\sqrt{N_{n,k}\log\log N_{n,k}})$ a.s.;
since $N_{n,k}\sim v_k n$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:match}), eventually $N_{n,k}\le 2v_k n$ and
$\log\log N_{n,k}\le 2\log\log n$, whence $|Q_{n,k}| = O(\sqrt{n\log\log n})$
(\texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_respMart\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_loglog}). Dividing by $N_{n,k}+1
\gtrsim (v_k/2)n$ bounds $|\hat{\theta}_{n,k}-\theta_k| \le
(2/v_k)(C+|\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k|)\sqrt{n\log\log n}/n = O(\sqrt{\log\log n / n})$, via the shared
deterministic core \texttt{abs\_estimator\_sub\_le\_rate\_gen}. The coarser $\log$-rate route through
the truncation LIL (Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_truncation}, \texttt{abs\_estimator\_sub\_le\_rate\_ae})
remains available.
nodes.name: Proof of LIL rate for the estimator
nodes.statement_short: Exact error identity plus the subsampled Hartman-Wintner LIL and linear growth of the counts.

nodes.statement:
Under the same hypotheses,
$\hat{\rho}_n - v = O\!\big(\sqrt{\tfrac{\log\log n}{n}}\big)$ and hence
$n(\hat{\rho}_n - v) = O(\sqrt{n\log\log n})$ a.s.
nodes.name: Rate for the plug-in target
nodes.label: lem:rho_rate

nodes.statement:
A first-order Taylor expansion of $\Target$ around $\Params$ (twice
differentiable by Condition~\textbf{B}) gives
$\hat{\rho}_n - v = G(\estParams_n-\Params) + O(\|\estParams_n-\Params\|^2)$
with $G := \nabla\Target|_\Params$. Both terms are
$O(\sqrt{\log\log n / n})$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_LIL}.

\emph{Formalization.} The delta-method core is formalized as \texttt{AlphaRAR.rho\_rate}: for a target
map $\Target$ merely \emph{differentiable} at $\Params$ (the first-order part of Condition~\textbf{B};
the second-order term is unnecessary for the $O$-rate), if the estimator vector converges,
$\estParams_n\to\Params$ a.s.\ (Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_consistent}), with each coordinate at the rate
$\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k = O(r_n)$ a.s.\ (Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_LIL}, $r_n=\sqrt{\log\log n/n}$),
then every coordinate of the plug-in target satisfies $\hat\rho_{n,k}-v_k = O(r_n)$ a.s. The
mechanism is the generic estimate \texttt{AlphaRAR.isBigO\_target\_sub\_of\_tendsto}: a differentiable
map sends $\estParams_n-\Params$ to $\Target(\estParams_n)-\Target(\Params)$ of the same big-$O$ order
(\texttt{AlphaRAR.isBigO\_sub\_comp\_of\_differentiableAt}, from \texttt{HasFDerivAt.isBigO\_sub}),
combined coordinatewise via \texttt{isBigO\_pi}. For a concrete aRTS design this is fully discharged in
\texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTS\_rho\_rate}: consistency $\estParams_n\to\Params$ is
\texttt{aRTS\_theta\_consistent} (Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_consistent}) and the coordinatewise rate is the
subsampled loglog LIL (Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_LIL}), fed through the positive allocation proportion, so
the only remaining hypotheses are Condition~\textbf{B} (differentiability and non-sparsity) and the
Condition~\textbf{A} moments.
nodes.name: Proof of Rate for the plug-in target
nodes.statement_short: First-order Taylor expansion of the target map transfers the estimator rate.

nodes.statement:
Under the generic conditions and Conditions~\textbf{A}--\textbf{B}, for every
$k\in[K]$, as $n\to\infty$,
\[
  \frac{N_{n,k}}{n}\xrightarrow{a.s.} v_k, \qquad
  \estParams_n - \Params = O\!\Big(\sqrt{\tfrac{\log\log n}{n}}\Big)\ \text{a.s.},\qquad
  n(\hat{\rho}_n - v) = O(\sqrt{n\log\log n})\ \text{a.s.}
\]
nodes.name: Strong consistency and rates
nodes.statement_short: Allocation proportions converge a.s. to the target; estimators and plug-in targets converge at the LIL rate.
assumptions: Under the generic conditions and Conditions~\textbf{A}--\textbf{B}
nodes.label: thm:LLN

nodes.statement:
Combine Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_consistent} (first statement), Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_LIL}
(second) and Lemma~\ref{lem:rho_rate} (third). The formalization \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTS\_LLN} bundles
the conclusions for an aRTS design: $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ (\texttt{aRTS\_proportion\_tendsto}),
$\hat\theta_{n,k}\to\theta_k$ (\texttt{aRTS\_theta\_consistent}),
$\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k=O(\sqrt{\log\log n/n})$ (\texttt{aRTS\_theta\_rate}, the
Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_LIL} rate instantiated for aRTS through the positive allocation proportion)
and $\hat\rho_{n,k}-v_k=O(\sqrt{\log\log n/n})$ (\texttt{aRTS\_rho\_rate}), under the aRTS design
hypotheses and Conditions~\textbf{A}--\textbf{B}.
nodes.name: Proof of Strong consistency and rates
nodes.statement_short: Combine the three preceding lemmas.

nodes.statement:
We introduce the notation
\[
  G := \nabla\Target\big|_\Params, \qquad
  V := \mathrm{diag}\!\Big(\tfrac{V_1}{v_1}, \dots, \tfrac{V_K}{v_K}\Big), \qquad
  \Omega := \begin{pmatrix} GVG^\top & GVG^\top\\ GVG^\top & GVG^\top\end{pmatrix}.
\]
