(\texttt{condExp\_genRespMart\_increment\_sq}), and these sum to $\sum_{i<n}v_i D_i$. (Unlike the
response martingale $Q$, whose constant variance gives $V_k N$, the truncated variances $v_i$ vary
with $i$, so the weighted sum is retained.)
nodes.name: Proof of Quadratic variation of $\tilde M$
nodes.statement_short: Instance of the general functional quadratic variation.

nodes.statement:
$\langle\tilde M\rangle_n\le V_k N_{n,k}$ a.s., since each $v_i\le V_k$ (truncation reduces the
absolute value, and variance is at most the second moment). This is the only bound on
$\langle\tilde M\rangle$ used by the block LIL argument (the matching lower bound and the
convergence $v_i\to\sigma^2$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_var_conv} are not needed for the $O$-rate).
nodes.name: Quadratic variation upper bound
nodes.label: lem:trunc_qv_le

nodes.name: Proof of Quadratic variation upper bound
nodes.statement_short: Truncated variance is at most the arm variance.

nodes.statement:
(Not needed for the $O$-rate.) $v_i\to\sigma^2$; in particular $\tfrac12\sigma^2\le v_i\le\sigma^2$
for all large $i$, so
$\tfrac12\sigma^2 N_n\le\langle\tilde M\rangle_n\le\sigma^2 N_n$ eventually and
$\langle\tilde M\rangle_n\asymp\sigma^2 N_n$.
nodes.name: Truncated variances converge
nodes.label: lem:trunc_var_conv

nodes.statement:
$v_i=\E[(\xi_i^{\mathrm t})^2]-m_i^2$. As $\sqrt i\to\infty$, $\E[(\xi_i^{\mathrm t})^2]
=\int\operatorname{trunc}(x-\theta_k,\sqrt i)^2\,d\nu_k\to\int(x-\theta_k)^2\,d\nu_k=\sigma^2$
by monotone/dominated convergence, and $m_i\to0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_mean_bound}), so
$v_i\to\sigma^2$. The upper bound $v_i\le\sigma^2$ is immediate from
$|\operatorname{trunc}(\xi_i,\sqrt i)|\le|\xi_i|$.
nodes.name: Proof of Truncated variances converge
nodes.statement_short: Monotone/dominated convergence for the truncated second moment.

nodes.statement:
On block $k$ we use horizon $2^k$, increment bound $c_k:=2\sqrt{2^k}$, and the \emph{constrained}
exponential parameter $\theta_k:=1/c_k$ (the optimizer is inadmissible).
nodes.section: 12.3.4 Core: the growing-increment LIL for $\tilde M$
nodes.name: Block increment bound and constrained parameter

nodes.statement:
Fix $C>0$ and set $\lambda_k:=C\sqrt{2^k\,k}$. For each $k$,
\[
  \Prob\!\Big(\exists\,m\le 2^k:\ \tilde M_m\ge\lambda_k,\ \langle\tilde M\rangle_m\le\sigma^2 2^k\Big)
  \le \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{C}{2}\sqrt k+\tfrac{\sigma^2}{4}\big).
\]
Here $\sigma^2=V_k$ is the arm variance and $\langle\tilde M\rangle_m\le V_k 2^k$ uses only the
upper bound Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_qv_le}.
nodes.section: 12.3.4 Core: the growing-increment LIL for $\tilde M$
nodes.name: Per-block Freedman with constrained $\theta$
nodes.label: lem:trunc_block

nodes.statement:
Apply the Freedman inequality (Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_freedman}) to the martingale stopped at time
$2^k$ --- whose increments are bounded by $c_k=2\sqrt{2^k}$, so $\theta_k c_k=1$ is admissible ---
with $\theta=\theta_k$, $\lambda=\lambda_k$, $v=\sigma^2 2^k$. The exponent is
$-\theta_k\lambda_k+\theta_k^2\sigma^2 2^k=-\tfrac C2\sqrt k+\tfrac{\sigma^2}4$, since
$\theta_k\lambda_k=\tfrac{C\sqrt{2^k k}}{2\sqrt{2^k}}=\tfrac C2\sqrt k$ and
$\theta_k^2\sigma^2 2^k=\tfrac{\sigma^2 2^k}{4\cdot2^k}=\tfrac{\sigma^2}4$. Stopping at $2^k$ is
needed so the increment bound holds up to the horizon; on the event only times $m\le 2^k$ occur,
where the stopped process agrees with $\tilde M$.

The formalization packages the stopping into a reusable device
\texttt{AlphaRAR.measure\_exists\_ge\_le\_exp\_horizon}: a version of the pre-optimization Freedman
bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_freedman}) whose increment bound $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ is required only for
$i<N$, and whose event is restricted to $m\le N$. It is proved by applying
Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_freedman} to the deterministically stopped process
$M^N_m:=M_{\min(m,N)}$ (Mathlib's \texttt{stoppedProcess} at the constant time $N$), which is a martingale
(\texttt{martingale\_stoppedProcess\_const}), whose increments vanish past $N$ hence are globally bounded by
$c$, and whose predictable quadratic variation agrees with $\langle M\rangle$ below the horizon
(\texttt{predQuadVar\_stoppedProcess\_const\_of\_le}). Here it is used with $N=2^k$, $c=c_k=2\sqrt{2^k}$, the
constrained $\theta_k=1/c_k$, and the increment bound $|\Delta\tilde M_i|\le2\sqrt i\le c_k$ for
$i<2^k$ (\texttt{abs\_truncRespMart\_increment\_le}).
nodes.section: 12.3.4 Core: the growing-increment LIL for $\tilde M$
nodes.name: Proof of Per-block Freedman with constrained $\theta$
nodes.statement_short: Freedman on the martingale stopped at 2^k with the constrained exponential parameter.

nodes.statement: For every $C>0$, $\sum_k \exp(-\tfrac C2\sqrt k+\tfrac{\sigma^2}4)<\infty$.
nodes.section: 12.3.4 Core: the growing-increment LIL for $\tilde M$
nodes.name: Block probabilities are summable
nodes.label: lem:trunc_block_summable

nodes.statement:
$\exp(-\tfrac C2\sqrt k)$ is summable in $k$: since $\log=o(\sqrt\cdot)$, eventually
$2\log k\le \tfrac C2\sqrt k$, so the terms are $\le k^{-2}$.
nodes.section: 12.3.4 Core: the growing-increment LIL for $\tilde M$
nodes.name: Proof of Block probabilities are summable
nodes.statement_short: Eventually the terms are at most k^-2.

nodes.statement:
$\tilde M_n=O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ a.s.

\textbf{Reusable tool.} The block argument is formalized \emph{abstractly}, for any $L^2$-martingale
$M$ with a square-root-growing increment bound $|\Delta M_i|\le a\sqrt i$ and a linear quadratic
variation bound $\langle M\rangle_n\le v\,n$: the general lemmas
\texttt{measure\_exists\_ge\_le\_exp\_block} (per-block Freedman),
\texttt{ae\_eventually\_lt\_block\_of\_growing} (block Borel--Cantelli),
\texttt{ae\_eventually\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_log\_of\_growing} (one-sided $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$) and
\texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_log\_of\_growing} (\emph{two-sided}, via $\pm M$ and
$\langle -M\rangle=\langle M\rangle$) live in \texttt{LILTruncation.lean} and belong upstream. The
truncated martingale $\tilde M$ is the instance $a=2$, $v=V_k$; in particular the two-sided form
\texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_truncRespMart\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_log} ($|\tilde M_n|\le
C\sqrt{n\log n}$) is free.
nodes.section: 12.3.4 Core: the growing-increment LIL for $\tilde M$
nodes.name: LIL for the truncated martingale
nodes.label: lem:trunc_mart_lil

nodes.statement:
Borel--Cantelli over the blocks (Lemmas~\ref{lem:trunc_block}--\ref{lem:trunc_block_summable})
gives that a.s.\ for all large $k$ and every $m\le 2^k$, $\langle\tilde M\rangle_m\le\sigma^2 2^k
\Rightarrow \tilde M_m<\lambda_k$ (formalized as
\texttt{ae\_eventually\_truncRespMart\_lt\_block}, the summable first Borel--Cantelli step). To
bound a fixed time $n$, take the \emph{least} $k$ with $n\le 2^k$; then $2^k\le 2n$ and
$k\le\log_2 n+1$, and the quadratic-variation bound $\langle\tilde M\rangle_n\le V_k N_{n,k}\le V_k
n\le V_k 2^k$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_qv_le}) supplies the block hypothesis at $m=n\le 2^k$, giving
$\tilde M_n<\lambda_k=C\sqrt{2^k k}\le C'\sqrt{n\log n}$.

\textbf{Scale.} Because the increment bound $|\Delta\tilde M_i|\le2\sqrt i$ \emph{grows}, the block
horizon $m\le 2^k$ forces the least admissible $k$ to satisfy $2^k\ge n$, so time-blocking delivers
the \emph{time} scale $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ rather than the variance scale
$O(\sqrt{\langle\tilde M\rangle_n\log\langle\tilde M\rangle_n})=O(\sqrt{N_n\log N_n})$ of the
displayed statement. The two coincide when arm $k$ is sampled a positive fraction of the time
($N_{n,k}\asymp n$, the regime of interest); the sharper variance-scale bound would require blocking
by the quadratic variation rather than by the natural time, and is not formalized. The time-scale
form is exactly parallel to the bounded-increment Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_upper_nat}
(\texttt{ae\_eventually\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_log}).
nodes.section: 12.3.4 Core: the growing-increment LIL for $\tilde M$
nodes.name: Proof of LIL for the truncated martingale
nodes.statement_short: Block Borel-Cantelli and the least dyadic block containing n.

nodes.statement:
$M_n = O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ a.s. The formalized statement is \emph{two-sided},
\texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_respMart\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_log} ($|M_n|\le C\sqrt{n\log n}$
eventually, a.s.), with the one-sided form its immediate corollary. The two-sidedness comes for free
from the reusable growing-increment LIL tool (see Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_mart_lil}).
nodes.name: Truncation to finite variance
nodes.label: lem:lil_truncation

nodes.statement:
By Definition~\ref{def:lil_trunc}, $M_n=\tilde M_n+R_n+\mathrm{Dr}_n$. The main term is
$O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_mart_lil}); the tail is $O(1)$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_tail_const}); the drift is $O(\sqrt{n})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_drift}).
Both remainders are $o(\sqrt{n\log n})$, so $M_n=O(\sqrt{n\log n})$. In the regime of interest
$N_{n,k}\asymp n$, this is the $O(\sqrt{N_n\log N_n})=O(\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\langle
M\rangle_n})$ rate (using $\langle M\rangle_n=\sigma^2 N_n$) required downstream.
nodes.name: Proof of Truncation to finite variance
nodes.statement_short: Three-term decomposition; main term LIL, tail O(1), drift O(sqrt n).

nodes.statement:
\textbf{Remark.} Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_truncation} is exactly the shape used in
Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_LIL}: there $M = Q_{\cdot,k}$, $D_i = X_{i,k}$,
$\xi_i = \xi_{i,k}-\theta_k$, and $\langle Q_{\cdot,k}\rangle_n = V_k N_{n,k}$, so
the conclusion reads $Q_{n,k} = O(\sqrt{N_{n,k}\log N_{n,k}})$ a.s. The same
statement applied to the bounded martingale $M_{\cdot,k}$
(Definition~\ref{def:M}) covers the use in Lemma~\ref{lem:U_increment_bound}; that direction is
already formalized as Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_upper_nat}.
nodes.name: Use of the truncation LIL in Part I
nodes.statement_short: The truncation LIL applied to Q gives the log-rate bound on the response martingale used for the estimator rate.

nodes.statement:
For every $\kappa>2$ and $\eta>1$,
$\sum_{k}\exp\!\big(-\tfrac{\kappa^2}{4}\log\log\eta^k\big)<\infty$. (Formalized with base $\eta=2$
and the surrogate $\log(k+2)\asymp\log\log 2^k$: for $1<p$, $\sum_k\exp(-p\log(k+2))<\infty$.)
nodes.name: $p$-series tail summability
nodes.label: lem:llil_tail_summable

nodes.statement:
For $k\ge1$, $\log\log\eta^k=\log(k\log\eta)$, so the $k$-th term equals
$(k\log\eta)^{-\kappa^2/4}=(\log\eta)^{-\kappa^2/4}\,k^{-\kappa^2/4}$. Since
$\kappa^2/4>1$ this is a convergent $p$-series (Mathlib
\texttt{summable\_one\_div\_nat\_rpow}); dropping the finitely many indices with
$\log\log\eta^k\le0$ does not affect summability.
nodes.name: Proof of $p$-series tail summability
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite as a convergent p-series.

nodes.statement:
Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$ and $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ a.e.
Let $(v_k),(\lambda_k)$ be positive schedules such that
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $\lambda_k c\le 2v_k$ for all large $k$ \emph{(eventual admissibility)}, and
  \item $\sum_k\exp(-\lambda_k^2/(4v_k))<\infty$.
\end{enumerate}
Then almost surely, for all large $k$ and every $n$,
$\langle M\rangle_n\le v_k\Rightarrow M_n<\lambda_k$.
nodes.name: Borel--Cantelli with eventual admissibility
nodes.label: lem:llil_evt_adm

nodes.statement:
As in Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_bc}, for indices $k$ where admissibility holds the optimized
Freedman bound (Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_freedman_opt}, infinite-horizon form
\texttt{measure\_exists\_ge\_le\_exp\_all}) gives
$\Prob(s_k)\le\exp(-\lambda_k^2/(4v_k))$, where
$s_k=\{\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda_k,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v_k\}$; for the finitely many
remaining $k$ use the trivial bound $\Prob(s_k)\le1$. The total $\sum_k\Prob(s_k)$ is
still finite, so the first Borel--Cantelli lemma (\texttt{ae\_eventually\_notMem})
places a.e.\ $\omega$ in only finitely many $s_k$; the complement is the claim. This is
Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_bc} with its ``$\forall k$'' admissibility weakened to
``$\forall^\infty k$''.
nodes.name: Proof of Borel--Cantelli with eventual admissibility
nodes.statement_short: Freedman bound for admissible indices, trivial bound for finitely many others, then Borel-Cantelli.

nodes.statement:
Let $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ a.e.\ with $c>0$. Fix $\eta>1$ and $\kappa>2$, set $v_k=\eta^k$
and $\lambda_k=\kappa\sqrt{\eta^k\,\log\log\eta^k}$ (for $k$ large enough that
$\log\log\eta^k>0$). Then almost surely, for all large $k$ and every $n$,
$\langle M\rangle_n\le\eta^k\Rightarrow M_n<\kappa\sqrt{\eta^k\log\log\eta^k}$.
(Formalized with $\eta=2$ and the surrogate $\lambda_k=\kappa\sqrt{2^k\log(k+2)}$.)
nodes.name: Bounded-increment $\log\log$ exceedance
nodes.label: lem:llil_bounded_block

nodes.statement:
Eventual admissibility: $\lambda_k c\le 2v_k$ reads
$\kappa c\sqrt{\log\log\eta^k/\eta^k}\le2$, which holds for large $k$ because
$\log\log\eta^k/\eta^k\to0$ (in the formalization, $\lambda_k c\le2\cdot2^k$ reduces to
$(\kappa c)^2\log(k+2)\le4\cdot2^k$, eventual since $\log(k+2)=o(2^k)$). Summability:
$\exp(-\lambda_k^2/(4v_k))=\exp(-\tfrac{\kappa^2}{4}\log\log\eta^k)$ is summable by
Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_tail_summable}. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_evt_adm}.
nodes.name: Proof of Bounded-increment $\log\log$ exceedance
nodes.statement_short: Check eventual admissibility and summability, then apply the relaxed Borel-Cantelli lemma.

nodes.statement:
Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$, $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ a.e., and
$\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$ a.s. Then for every constant $C>2$, almost surely
\[
  M_n\le C\,\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\,\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}\qquad
  \text{for all large }n.
\]
nodes.name: General bounded-increment LIL, $O$-rate
assumptions: Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$, $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ a.e., and $\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$ a.s.
nodes.label: thm:llil_bounded

nodes.statement:
Pick $\eta>1$ and $\kappa\in(2,C/\sqrt\eta)$ (possible once $\eta<(C/2)^2$), and use
Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_bounded_block}. For large $n$ let $k$ be the least index with
$\langle M\rangle_n\le\eta^k$; minimality gives $\eta^k\le\eta\langle M\rangle_n$, and
$\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$ makes $\log\log\eta^k\le\log\log(\eta\langle M\rangle_n)
\le(1+o(1))\log\log\langle M\rangle_n$. Hence
$M_n<\kappa\sqrt{\eta^k\log\log\eta^k}\le\kappa\sqrt\eta\,(1+o(1))
\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}\le C\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n
\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}$ for large $n$.
nodes.name: Proof of General bounded-increment LIL, $O$-rate
nodes.statement_short: Block lemma plus repackaging via the least eta^k above <M>_n.

nodes.statement:
$M$ satisfies \textbf{(H)} with constant $A>0$ if there is an $\filt$-predictable
sequence $(c_i)$ with $|\Delta M_i|\le c_i$ a.e.\ and, for all large $i$,
\[
  c_i\ \le\ A\,\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_i\,/\,\log\log\langle M\rangle_i}\qquad\text{a.e.}
\]
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.name: Condition \textbf{(H)}
nodes.statement_short: Increments small on the LIL scale relative to the quadratic variation.
nodes.label: def:llil_H

nodes.statement:
A fixed bound $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ satisfies \textbf{(H)} with \emph{every} $A>0$ once
$\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$, since then $\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_i/\log\log\langle
M\rangle_i}\to\infty$.
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.name: Bounded increments satisfy (H)

nodes.statement:
This is the standard device of the martingale LIL \cite{Stout1970,HallHeyde1980} (see also
\cite{Freedman1975} for the underlying exponential inequality): the geometric \emph{block base}
must act on the quadratic variation itself (via a random stopping time), \emph{not} on a
deterministic time horizon. A deterministic-horizon blocking $2^j$ (as in the $O$-rate engine of
Chapter~\ref{chap:pre_lil}) unavoidably loses a factor $\sqrt2$ in the constant when passing to the
$\langle M\rangle_n$ scale, so it yields the $O$-rate but never the sharp constant~$1$; the
sharp constant requires block base $\eta\downarrow1$ on $\langle M\rangle$, which is exactly this
quadratic-variation stopping.
For $v>0$ let $\tau_v:=\inf\{n:\ \langle M\rangle_{n+1}>v\}$. Because $\langle M\rangle$
is predictable ($\langle M\rangle_{n+1}$ is $\filt_n$-measurable), $\tau_v$ is a
stopping time, and on $\{n\le\tau_v\}$ one has $\langle M\rangle_n\le v$. The stopped
process $M^{\tau_v}_n:=M_{n\wedge\tau_v}$ is a martingale with
$\langle M^{\tau_v}\rangle_n=\langle M\rangle_{n\wedge\tau_v}$, and under \textbf{(H)}
with constant $A$ its increments obey $|\Delta M^{\tau_v}_i|\le C(v):=A\sqrt{v/\log\log v}$
a.e.\ for all $i$ (for $v$ large), since for $i<\tau_v$ we have $\langle M\rangle_i\le v$
and past $\tau_v$ the increments vanish. Moreover
\[
  \{\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v\}\ \subseteq\
  \{\exists n:\ M^{\tau_v}_n\ge\lambda,\ \langle M^{\tau_v}\rangle_n\le v\}.
\]
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.name: Quadratic-variation stopping
nodes.statement_short: Stopping when the quadratic variation exceeds v yields a martingale with small increments covering the block event.
nodes.label: lem:llil_qv_stop

nodes.statement:
Predictability of $\langle M\rangle$ gives $\{\tau_v\ge n+1\}=\{\langle M\rangle_{n+1}
\le v\}\in\filt_n$, so $\tau_v$ is a stopping time (constructible with Mathlib's
\texttt{hittingBtwn}, the stopping-time API already used in the proof of Ville's
inequality). That $M^{\tau_v}$ is a martingale is Mathlib's
\texttt{Submartingale.stoppedProcess} applied to $\pm M$; the increment bound uses
monotonicity of $\langle M\rangle$ and \textbf{(H)}. The only genuinely new ingredient is
the quadratic-variation identity $\langle M^{\tau_v}\rangle=\langle M\rangle_{\cdot\wedge
\tau_v}$, the stopping-time analogue of the \emph{formalized} deterministic-horizon
\texttt{predQuadVar\_stoppedProcess\_const\_of\_le} of Chapter~\ref{chap:pre_lil}. For the inclusion: if
$\langle M\rangle_n\le v$ then $n\le\tau_v$, so $M^{\tau_v}_n=M_n$ and
$\langle M^{\tau_v}\rangle_n=\langle M\rangle_n$.
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.name: Proof of Quadratic-variation stopping
nodes.statement_short: Predictability makes tau a stopping time; stopped process inherits martingale property and small increments.

nodes.statement:
Suppose $M$ satisfies \textbf{(H)} with constant $A$. Fix $\kappa>0$ with
$\kappa A\le2$, set $v_k=\eta^k$ ($\eta>1$) and
$\lambda_k=\kappa\sqrt{v_k\log\log v_k}$. Then for all large $k$,
\[
  \Prob\big(\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda_k,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v_k\big)\ \le\
  \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{\kappa^2}{4}\log\log v_k\big).
\]
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.name: Per-block bound under \textbf{(H)}
nodes.label: lem:llil_H_measure

nodes.statement:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_qv_stop} the event is contained in the corresponding event for
the stopped martingale $M^{\tau_{v_k}}$, whose increments are globally bounded by
$C(v_k)=A\sqrt{v_k/\log\log v_k}$. Apply the optimized infinite-horizon Freedman bound
(Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_freedman_opt}) to $M^{\tau_{v_k}}$ with $c=C(v_k)$,
$\lambda=\lambda_k$, $v=v_k$: admissibility $\lambda_k C(v_k)\le2v_k$ reads
$\kappa\sqrt{v_k\log\log v_k}\cdot A\sqrt{v_k/\log\log v_k}=\kappa A\,v_k\le2v_k$, i.e.\
$\kappa A\le2$; and the exponent is
$-\lambda_k^2/(4v_k)=-\tfrac{\kappa^2}{4}\log\log v_k$.
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.name: Proof of Per-block bound under \textbf{(H)}
nodes.statement_short: Stop at the quadratic-variation level and apply the optimized Freedman bound.

nodes.statement:
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_H_measure} with additionally $\kappa>2$
(so $A<1$ and $A\le2/\kappa$), almost surely for all large $k$ and every $n$,
$\langle M\rangle_n\le\eta^k\Rightarrow M_n<\kappa\sqrt{\eta^k\log\log\eta^k}$.
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.name: \textbf{(H)} exceedance
nodes.label: lem:llil_H_block

nodes.statement:
The per-block bounds of Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_H_measure} are summable by
Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_tail_summable} ($\kappa>2$), so $\sum_k\Prob(s_k)<\infty$ with
$s_k=\{\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda_k,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v_k\}$; the first
Borel--Cantelli lemma finishes as in Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_evt_adm}.
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.name: Proof of \textbf{(H)} exceedance
nodes.statement_short: Summable per-block bounds and Borel-Cantelli.

nodes.statement:
Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$ satisfying \textbf{(H)} with some
constant $A<1$, and $\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$ a.s. Then there is a constant $C$
(any $C>2$ suffices, once $A$ is small enough) such that almost surely
\[
  M_n\le C\,\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\,\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}\qquad
  \text{for all large }n.
\]
Bounded increments (Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_bounded}) are the case $A\to0$.
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.name: General martingale LIL under \textbf{(H)}, $O$-rate
nodes.label: thm:llil_general

nodes.statement:
Choose $\kappa>2$ with $\kappa A\le2$ and $\eta>1$, apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_H_block}, and repackage exactly as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_bounded} (least $k$ with $\langle M\rangle_n\le\eta^k$).
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.name: Proof of General martingale LIL under \textbf{(H)}, $O$-rate
nodes.statement_short: Block exceedance lemma under (H) and repackaging.

nodes.statement:
For every $\delta>0$ there is $\eta_\delta>0$ such that $e^x\le1+x+\tfrac12(1+\delta)x^2$
for all $|x|\le\eta_\delta$.
nodes.name: Refined elementary inequality
nodes.label: lem:llil_refined_ineq

nodes.statement:
Mathlib's \texttt{Real.exp\_bound} at $n=3$ gives, for $|x|\le1$,
$\big|e^x-(1+x+\tfrac12 x^2)\big|\le|x|^3\cdot\tfrac{4}{3!\cdot3}=\tfrac29|x|^3$, hence
$e^x\le1+x+\tfrac12 x^2+\tfrac29|x|^3\le1+x+\tfrac12\big(1+\tfrac49|x|\big)x^2$; take
$\eta_\delta:=\min(1,\tfrac94\delta)$. (So this lemma is a Mathlib one-liner, not new work.)
nodes.name: Proof of Refined elementary inequality
nodes.statement_short: Mathlib's exponential bound at order three.

nodes.statement:
If $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ a.e.\ and $|\theta|c\le\eta_\delta$, then
$\E[e^{\theta\Delta M_i}\mid\filt_i]\le\exp\!\big(\tfrac12(1+\delta)\theta^2
(\langle M\rangle_{i+1}-\langle M\rangle_i)\big)$ a.e.
nodes.name: Refined conditional MGF bound
nodes.label: lem:llil_refined_mgf

nodes.statement:
As in Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_exp_supermart}'s one-step bound, but with
Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_refined_ineq} in place of $e^x\le1+x+x^2$: using
$\E[\Delta M_i\mid\filt_i]=0$ and $\E[(\Delta M_i)^2\mid\filt_i]=\langle M\rangle_{i+1}
-\langle M\rangle_i$, one gets
$\E[e^{\theta\Delta M_i}\mid\filt_i]\le1+\tfrac12(1+\delta)\theta^2
(\langle M\rangle_{i+1}-\langle M\rangle_i)\le\exp(\cdots)$.
nodes.name: Proof of Refined conditional MGF bound
nodes.statement_short: Same as the crude MGF bound with the refined inequality.

nodes.statement:
Under $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ and $|\theta|c\le\eta_\delta$, the process
$Z_n=\exp\!\big(\theta M_n-\tfrac12(1+\delta)\theta^2\langle M\rangle_n\big)$ is a
supermartingale, and hence for $\lambda,v>0$,
\[
  \Prob\big(\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v\big)\ \le\
  \exp\!\big(-\theta\lambda+\tfrac12(1+\delta)\theta^2 v\big).
\]
Optimizing at $\theta=\lambda/((1+\delta)v)$ (admissible when
$\lambda c\le(1+\delta)v\,\eta_\delta$) gives the bound
$\exp\!\big(-\lambda^2/(2(1+\delta)v)\big)$.
nodes.name: Refined exponential supermartingale and Freedman bound
nodes.label: lem:llil_refined_freedman

nodes.statement:
Verbatim the proofs of Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_exp_supermart} (supermartingale, via
Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_refined_mgf}), Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_freedman} (Ville's inequality),
and Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_freedman_opt} (optimization), with the proxy $2v$ replaced
by $(1+\delta)v$.
nodes.name: Proof of Refined exponential supermartingale and Freedman bound
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the supermartingale, Ville and optimization steps with the refined proxy.

nodes.statement:
Let $M$ satisfy \textbf{(H)} with constant $A$ (or have bounded increments), and
$\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$. Fix $\eta>1$ and $\varepsilon>\delta>0$, set $v_k=\eta^k$
and $\lambda_k=\sqrt{2(1+\varepsilon)\,v_k\log\log v_k}$. Then almost surely for all
large $k$ and every $n$,
$\langle M\rangle_n\le\eta^k\Rightarrow M_n<\sqrt{2(1+\varepsilon)\eta^k\log\log\eta^k}$.
(Formalized for bounded increments, with the surrogate $\log(k+2)\asymp\log\log\eta^k$ in place of
$\log\log\eta^k$, which is asymptotically equal and so preserves the sharp constant.)
nodes.name: Sharp exceedance
nodes.label: lem:llil_sharp_block

nodes.statement:
Stop at $\tau_{v_k}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_qv_stop}); the stopped increments are bounded
by $C(v_k)=A\sqrt{v_k/\log\log v_k}$ (or by the fixed $c$). The optimizer
$\theta_k=\lambda_k/((1+\delta)v_k)=\sqrt{2(1+\varepsilon)\log\log v_k/v_k}/(1+\delta)$
satisfies $\theta_k C(v_k)=A\sqrt{2(1+\varepsilon)}/(1+\delta)$, which is $\le\eta_\delta$
for $A$ small (bounded case: $\theta_k c\to0$). Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_refined_freedman}
gives $\Prob(s_k)\le\exp(-\lambda_k^2/(2(1+\delta)v_k))
=\exp(-\tfrac{1+\varepsilon}{1+\delta}\log\log v_k)$, summable by
Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_tail_summable}'s argument since $(1+\varepsilon)/(1+\delta)>1$.
Borel--Cantelli finishes.
nodes.name: Proof of Sharp exceedance
nodes.statement_short: Stop at the quadratic-variation level, refined Freedman bound, summability, Borel-Cantelli.

nodes.statement:
Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$, $\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$
a.s., satisfying \textbf{(H)} (in particular any bounded-increment martingale). Then
\[
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{M_n}{\sqrt{2\,\langle M\rangle_n\,\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}}
  \ \le\ 1\qquad\text{a.s.},
\]
and, applied to $-M$ (same quadratic variation, Definition~\ref{def:pred_qv}), the two-sided
bound $\limsup_n|M_n|/\sqrt{2\langle M\rangle_n\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}\le1$ a.s.
(Formalized for bounded increments, both in the equivalent form ``a.s.\ for every $b>1$, eventually
$|M_n|\le b\sqrt{2\langle M\rangle_n\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}$'' and as the genuine
$\limsup$ statement \texttt{AlphaRAR.ae\_limsup\_abs\_div\_sqrt\_predQuadVar\_mul\_loglog\_le\_one}.)
nodes.name: Sharp general martingale LIL
nodes.statement_short: Sharp-constant martingale LIL under condition (H).
assumptions: Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$, $\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$ a.s., satisfying \textbf{(H)}
nodes.label: thm:llil_sharp

nodes.statement:
Fix a countable family $\eta_j\downarrow1$, $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$ with
$\varepsilon_j>\delta_j>0$. For each $j$, Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_sharp_block} and the
repackaging of Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_bounded} give, a.s.,
$\limsup_n M_n/\sqrt{2\langle M\rangle_n\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}\le
\sqrt{(1+\varepsilon_j)\eta_j}$. Intersect the countably many a.s.\ events and let
$j\to\infty$.
nodes.name: Proof of Sharp general martingale LIL
nodes.statement_short: Countable family of parameters tending to the sharp values; intersect a.s. events.

nodes.statement:
Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$, increments bounded by a monotone
nonnegative growth $|\Delta M_i|\le g(i)$ satisfying the base-independent condition
\textbf{(H)} $g(n)\sqrt{L(n)/n}\to0$, and a \emph{linear} quadratic-variation bound
$\langle M\rangle_n\le v\,n$ ($v>0$). Then, a.s., for every $\beta>1$ eventually
$|M_n|\le\beta\sqrt{2v\,n\,L(n)}$, i.e.\ $\limsup_n|M_n|/\sqrt{2v\,n\,L(n)}\le1$.
nodes.name: Sharp LIL for growing increments with a linear quadratic variation
nodes.statement_short: Sharp LIL for growing increments when the quadratic variation grows linearly.
nodes.label: thm:llil_growth_sharp

nodes.statement:
Fix $\beta>1$ and block with the geometric horizons $N_j=\lceil\rho^j\rceil$ for
$\rho=1+(\beta-1)/2\downarrow1$ and $\delta=(\beta-1)/2$, so $(1+\delta)\rho=\rho^2<\beta^2$.
Over each block the increments are bounded by $g(N_j)$, and condition \textbf{(H)} transfers
to the block form $g(N_j)\sqrt{\log(j+2)/N_j}\to0$ because
$\log(j+2)\le(\log K+1)\,L(N_j)$ with $K=1/\log\rho+2$ (from $j\le\log N_j/\log\rho$), so the
block quantity is $\le\sqrt{\log K+1}\,g(N_j)\sqrt{L(N_j)/N_j}\to0$. The refined per-block
Freedman bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_sharp_block}) with the near-optimal
$\theta_j=\alpha\sqrt{\log(j+2)/N_j}$, $\alpha=C/((1+\delta)v)$, gives a summable
$p$-series tail; repackaging via the least $j$ with $n\le N_j$ (so $N_j\le\rho n+1$ and
additively $\log(j+2)\le D_\rho+L(n)$) yields the constant $\beta$. \emph{No random
stopping time}: the linear bound $\langle M\rangle_n\le v\,n$ lets the deterministic horizon
$N_j$ play the role of quadratic-variation stopping (contrast the general \textbf{(H)}
Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_sharp}, whose constant-\textbf{(H)} increments would require it).
Countable intersection over $\beta_m=1+1/(m+1)\downarrow1$ and the two-sided step (apply to
$-M$) give the $\limsup$ form.
nodes.name: Proof of Sharp LIL for growing increments with a linear quadratic variation
nodes.statement_short: Deterministic geometric horizons with ratio tending to one play the role of quadratic-variation stopping.

nodes.statement:
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_general} (or \ref{thm:llil_bounded}),
almost surely $|M_n|\le C\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}$ for all
large $n$, some deterministic $C$. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_bounded} to $M$ and $-M$.
(Formalized for bounded increments; the \textbf{(H)} version follows once
Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_general} is formalized.)
nodes.name: Two-sided normalized bound
nodes.label: cor:llil_norm

nodes.statement:
If moreover $\langle M\rangle_n\le K n$ for a constant $K$ (e.g.\ $|\Delta M_i|\le c$
gives $\langle M\rangle_n\le c^2 n$, Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_linear_bound}), then almost
surely $|M_n|\le C'\sqrt{n\log\log n}$ for all large $n$.
nodes.name: Bound at scale $\sqrt{n\log\log n}$
nodes.label: cor:llil_nat

nodes.statement:
$\langle M\rangle_n\le Kn$ gives $\log\log\langle M\rangle_n\le\log\log(Kn)\le
\log\log n+o(1)$ for large $n$; substitute into Corollary~\ref{cor:llil_norm}.
nodes.name: Proof of Bound at scale $\sqrt{n\log\log n}$
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the linear quadratic-variation bound into the normalized bound.

nodes.statement:
The normalized Corollary~\ref{cor:llil_norm} (\texttt{AlphaRAR.ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_sqrt\_pred
QuadVar\_mul\_loglog}) --- and hence \texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_loglog} ---
carries the standing hypothesis $\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$. For a \emph{bounded-increment}
martingale this hypothesis is \emph{unnecessary and can genuinely fail}: a deterministic path (all
selection probabilities in $\{0,1\}$) has $\langle M\rangle\equiv0$, yet $M\equiv0$ is trivially
$O(\sqrt{n\log\log n})$. The version \texttt{AlphaRAR.ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_loglog
\_of\_bdd} drops $\langle M\rangle\to\infty$ entirely: it applies the deterministic-horizon
growing-increment engine \texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_loglog\_of\_growing}, whose
only quadratic-variation input is the \emph{linear} bound $\langle M\rangle_n\le c^2n$
(\texttt{predQuadVar\_le\_of\_bound}), with parameters $\alpha=1/c$, $C=3c$, $v=c^2$ satisfying its
admissibility (via $\log(j+2)\le 2^j$) and summability (exponent $1<2$). This is the form the
possibly-degenerate assignment martingale requires.
nodes.name: The bounded-increment version is unconditional
nodes.label: rem:llil_bdd_uncond

nodes.statement:
Let $(Y_j)_{j\ge1}$ be i.i.d., $\E[Y_1]=0$, $\E[Y_1^2]=\sigma^2<\infty$, and
$S_m=\sum_{j\le m}Y_j$.
nodes.name: i.i.d. partial sum setting

nodes.statement:
With its natural filtration $S$ is a martingale with
$\langle S\rangle_m=\sigma^2 m$.
nodes.name: i.i.d. partial sum is a martingale with linear bracket
conclusions:
$S$ is a martingale with
$\langle S\rangle_m=\sigma^2 m$

nodes.statement: Write $L(t):=\log\log t$.
nodes.name: Iterated logarithm L

nodes.statement:
Let $(Y_j)_{j\ge0}$ be independent, integrable and centred ($\E Y_j=0$). Then the partial sums
$S_n=\sum_{j<n}Y_j$ are a martingale with $S_0=0$, for the ``strictly before $n$'' natural filtration
$\filt_n=\sigma(Y_0,\dots,Y_{n-1})$ (with $\filt_0$ trivial).
nodes.name: Partial sums of independent centred variables form a martingale
nodes.label: lem:hw_martingale

nodes.statement:
$S_n$ is $\filt_n$-measurable (a sum of $Y_0,\dots,Y_{n-1}$) and integrable. For the increment,
$\E[S_{n+1}\mid\filt_n]=S_n+\E[Y_n\mid\filt_n]=S_n+\E Y_n=S_n$, because $Y_n$ is independent of the
past $\filt_n=\sigma(Y_0,\dots,Y_{n-1})$. Mathlib's $\log\log$-free
\texttt{condExp\_indep\_eq} supplies $\E[Y_n\mid\filt_n]=\E Y_n$; the ``strictly before'' index is
what makes $S_0=0$ (unlike \texttt{Filtration.natural}, which would force $S_0=Y_0$).
nodes.name: Proof of Partial sums of independent centred variables form a martingale
nodes.statement_short: Independence gives the conditional increment its unconditional mean zero.

nodes.statement:
In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_martingale}, if additionally $\E[Y_j^2]<\infty$, the predictable
quadratic variation has increment $\langle S\rangle_{n+1}-\langle S\rangle_n=\E[Y_n^2]$; hence if
$\E[Y_j^2]\le v$ for all $j$, then $\langle S\rangle_n\le v\,n$ almost surely for all $n$.
nodes.name: Quadratic variation of the i.i.d.\ sum
nodes.label: lem:hw_qv

nodes.statement:
The increment of $\langle S\rangle$ is the conditional second moment of $\Delta S_n=Y_n$
(\texttt{predQuadVar\_succ\_sub\_eq}), which independence makes the constant $\E[Y_n^2]$
(\texttt{condExp\_natFiltLT\_comp\_indep} with $g=(\cdot)^2$); telescoping from $\langle S\rangle_0=0$
gives $\langle S\rangle_n=\sum_{j<n}\E[Y_j^2]\le v\,n$. Applied with $S=\tilde S$ and $v=\sigma^2$
(since $\Var(Y_j^{\mathrm L})\le\sigma^2$) this is the linear bound $\langle\tilde S\rangle_n\le
\sigma^2 n$ the growing-increment LIL requires.
nodes.name: Proof of Quadratic variation of the i.i.d.\ sum
nodes.statement_short: Compensator increments are the constant second moments; telescope.

nodes.statement:
Let $(Y_j)$ be independent and centred with $|Y_j|\le c$ a.e.\ and second moments bounded below,
$\E[Y_j^2]\ge w>0$. Then $S_n=\sum_{j<n}Y_j$ satisfies $|S_n|=O(\sqrt{n\log\log n})$ a.s.
nodes.name: Loglog LIL for bounded i.i.d.\ increments
nodes.label: cor:hw_bounded

nodes.statement:
$S$ is a martingale (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_martingale}) with bounded increments $|\Delta S_j|=|Y_j|\le c$;
its quadratic variation is $\langle S\rangle_n=\sum_{j<n}\E[Y_j^2]$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_qv}), so
$\langle S\rangle_n\ge w\,n\to\infty$. The bounded-increment loglog LIL
(Corollary~\ref{cor:llil_nat}) applies directly. This is the special case of
Theorem~\ref{thm:hw} where no truncation is needed, and is already fully formalized.
nodes.name: Proof of Loglog LIL for bounded i.i.d.\ increments
nodes.statement_short: Bounded-increment loglog LIL applied to the partial-sum martingale.

nodes.statement:
Low cutoff $b_j:=\sqrt{j/\log(j+2)}$ (the \emph{log}-level scale, strictly below the LIL
scale $\sqrt{j/L(j)}$) and high cutoff $\sqrt j$. Split each increment into low, medium and
high parts,
\[
  Y_j^{\mathrm L}:=Y_j\indic_{\{|Y_j|\le b_j\}},\quad
  Y_j^{\mathrm M}:=Y_j\indic_{\{b_j<|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}},\quad
  Y_j^{\mathrm H}:=Y_j\indic_{\{|Y_j|>\sqrt j\}},
\]
so $Y_j=Y_j^{\mathrm L}+Y_j^{\mathrm M}+Y_j^{\mathrm H}$, and set
\[
  \tilde S_m:=\sum_{j\le m}\!\big(Y_j^{\mathrm L}-\E Y_j^{\mathrm L}\big),\quad
  W_m:=\sum_{j\le m}\!\big(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\E Y_j^{\mathrm M}\big),\quad
  H_m:=\sum_{j\le m}Y_j^{\mathrm H},\quad
  D_m:=\sum_{j\le m}\E\big[Y_j\indic_{\{|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}}\big].
\]
Since $\E Y_j^{\mathrm L}+\E Y_j^{\mathrm M}=\E[Y_j\indic_{\{|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}}]$, one has
$S_m=\tilde S_m+W_m+H_m+D_m$.
nodes.name: Three-level truncated decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Three-level truncation of i.i.d. increments into low, medium and high parts plus drift.
nodes.label: def:hw_trunc

nodes.statement:
Almost surely $Y_j^{\mathrm H}=0$ for all large $j$, so $H_m$ is eventually constant and
$H_m=O(1)$ a.s. (The formalized statement is the equivalent substance: almost surely
$|Y_j|\le\sqrt j$ for all large $j$, whence $Y_j^{\mathrm H}=Y_j\indic_{\{|Y_j|>\sqrt j\}}=0$.)
nodes.name: High part is eventually zero
nodes.label: lem:hw_high

nodes.statement:
$\sum_j\Prob(|Y_j|>\sqrt j)=\sum_j\Prob(Y_1^2>j)\le\E[Y_1^2]+1<\infty$ by the layer-cake
bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_tail_summable}). The first Borel--Cantelli lemma places a.e.\
$\omega$ in only finitely many $\{|Y_j|>\sqrt j\}$; past that index $Y_j^{\mathrm H}=0$.
nodes.name: Proof of High part is eventually zero
nodes.statement_short: Layer-cake summability and Borel-Cantelli.

nodes.statement:
$\tilde S$ is a martingale with $|\Delta\tilde S_j|\le2b_j$ and $\langle\tilde
S\rangle_m=\sum_{j<m}\Var(Y_j^{\mathrm L})\le\sigma^2 m$. With the log-level cutoff
$b_j=\sqrt{j/\log(j+2)}$ the increments satisfy condition \textbf{(H)} in the sharp
$\to0$ form, $2b_n\sqrt{L(n)/n}=2\sqrt{L(n)/\log(n+2)}\to0$, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_growth_sharp} gives, a.s., for every $\beta>1$ eventually
$|\tilde S_m|\le\beta\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}$, i.e.\
$\limsup_m|\tilde S_m|/\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}\le1$.
nodes.name: Sharp low-part LIL
nodes.label: lem:hw_low_H

nodes.statement:
$|\Delta\tilde S_j|=|Y_j^{\mathrm L}-\E Y_j^{\mathrm L}|\le2b_j$
(\texttt{abs\_truncation\_sub\_integral\_le}), with $j\mapsto b_j$ monotone and
nonnegative; the base-independent condition \textbf{(H)} $2b_n\sqrt{L(n)/n}=
2\sqrt{L(n)/\log(n+2)}\to0$ holds because $L(n)/\log(n+2)\to0$. The martingale $\tilde S$
(\texttt{martingale\_centeredTruncation}) has the linear quadratic-variation bound
$\langle\tilde S\rangle_m\le\sigma^2 m$ (\texttt{predQuadVar\_centeredTruncation\_le}, via
\texttt{integral\_truncation\_sub\_integral\_sq\_le} for $\Var(Y^{\mathrm L})\le\sigma^2$).
These three feed the sharp growing-increment engine
(\texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_loglog\_of\_growth\_sharp\_all}) with growth
$g=2b$; the block scheme uses deterministic horizons $N_j=\lceil\rho^j\rceil$ with $\rho\downarrow1$,
so \emph{no random stopping time} is needed --- the linear bound $\langle\tilde S\rangle\le\sigma^2 m$
lets a deterministic time horizon play the role of quadratic-variation stopping. The upper bound uses
only $\langle\tilde S\rangle_m\le\sigma^2 m$; that $\Var(Y_j^{\mathrm L})\to\sigma^2$ (so
$\langle\tilde S\rangle_m/(\sigma^2 m)\to1$) is not needed for $\limsup\le1$, but confirms the
constant is sharp.
nodes.name: Proof of Sharp low-part LIL
nodes.statement_short: Verify the increment bound, condition (H) and linear quadratic variation, then apply the sharp growing-increment LIL.

nodes.statement: $\displaystyle\sum_{j\ge3}\frac{\Var(Y_j^{\mathrm M})}{j\,L(j)}<\infty$.
nodes.name: Medium variance series converges under a bare second moment
nodes.statement_short: The medium-band variance series against the LIL scale converges under a bare second moment.
nodes.label: lem:hw_medium_var

nodes.statement:
$\Var(Y_j^{\mathrm M})\le\E[(Y_j^{\mathrm M})^2]=\E[Y^2\indic_{\{b_j<|Y|\le\sqrt j\}}]$,
so by Tonelli
\[
  \sum_{j\ge3}\frac{\Var(Y_j^{\mathrm M})}{j\,L(j)}\ \le\
  \E\Big[Y^2\!\!\sum_{j:\,b_j<|Y|\le\sqrt j}\frac{1}{j\,L(j)}\Big].
\]
Fix $y=|Y|$. With the log-level cutoff $b_j=\sqrt{j/\log(j+2)}$ the condition
$b_j<y\le\sqrt j$ means $y^2\le j$ and $j/\log(j+2)<y^2$; as $t\mapsto t/\log(t+2)$ is
increasing the latter is $j<j_0(y)$, where $j_0(y)/\log(j_0(y)+2)=y^2$, so
$j_0(y)\asymp y^2\log(y^2)$. Thus $j$ runs over $[y^2,j_0(y))$, an interval of
multiplicative width $\asymp\log(y^2)$ on which $L(j)\asymp L(y^2)$; hence
\[
  \sum_{y^2\le j<j_0(y)}\frac{1}{j\,L(j)}\ \asymp\
  \frac{1}{L(y^2)}\log\frac{j_0(y)}{y^2}\ \asymp\
  \frac{\log\log(y^2)}{L(y^2)}\ =\ O(1),
\]
bounded uniformly in $y$. The inner factor being bounded, the double sum is
$\le C\,\E[Y^2]<\infty$. The mechanism: the medium band is only a $\log$-factor wide, so
the harmonic inner sum is $O(\log\log/\log\log)=O(1)$; this is exactly where the bare
second moment suffices. (The LIL-scale low cutoff $\sqrt{j/L(j)}$ would make the band a
mere $\log\log$-factor wide and the inner sum $\to0$; the log-level cutoff trades that
slack for the sharp-constant condition \textbf{(H)}$\to0$ of the low part, and $O(1)$
still gives convergence.)

\emph{Formalization.} Both the analytic heart and the measure-theoretic wrapper are formalized.
The uniform inner-sum bound $\sum_{j:\,t\le j<t\log(j+2)}1/(j\,L(j))\le C$ (with $t=y^2$) is
\texttt{AlphaRAR.medium\_inner\_tsum\_le}, built from \texttt{AlphaRAR.medium\_sum\_Icc\_big} (the
$t\ge9$ estimate: pull out $1/L(\lceil t\rceil)$ and bound the harmonic sum by
$\log(B/A)\le\log(5\log t)=\log5+L(t)$) via the range bounds \texttt{medium\_crude} ($j<8t^2$) and
\texttt{medium\_tight} ($j<t(\log9+2\log t)$), the harmonic comparison
\texttt{sum\_Icc\_one\_div\_le}, and \texttt{loglog\_le\_loglog}. The wrapper
\texttt{AlphaRAR.medium\_variance\_series\_le} turns it into the second-moment series: by finite-sum
linearity $\sum_{j<n}\big(\int X^2\indic_{\{b_j<|X|\le\sqrt j\}}\big)/(j\,L(j))=\int X^2\sum_{j<n}
\indic_{\{\dots\}}/(j\,L(j))$, the inner sum is $\le C$ pointwise (at $t=X(\omega)^2$, using
$b_j<|x|\le\sqrt j\iff x^2\le j<x^2\log(j+2)$), so each partial sum is $\le C\,\E[X^2]$ and
$\sum'_j(\dots)\le C\,\E[X^2]$ with the series summable. The reduction
$\Var(X\indic_{\{b_j<|X|\le\sqrt j\}})\le\E[(X\indic_{\{\dots\}})^2]=\E[X^2\indic_{\{\dots\}}]$
(\texttt{variance\_le\_expectation\_sq}, $(X\indic_S)^2=X^2\indic_S$) plus comparison of nonnegative
series (\texttt{Summable.of\_nonneg\_of\_le}) gives \texttt{AlphaRAR.medium\_variance\_summable}:
$\sum_{j\ge3}\Var(X\indic_{\{b_j<|X|\le\sqrt j\}})/(j\,L(j))<\infty$. Taking $X=Y_0$ and using
$\Var(Y_j^{\mathrm M})=\Var(Y_0\indic_{\{b_j<|Y_0|\le\sqrt j\}})$ (identical distribution) is the
stated series.
nodes.name: Proof of Medium variance series converges under a bare second moment
nodes.statement_short: Tonelli reduces to an inner harmonic sum over a log-wide band, bounded uniformly.

nodes.statement:
$W_m=o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$ a.s. (precisely, $W_m/\sqrt{2(m+3)L(m+3)}\to0$, and
$\sqrt{2(m+3)L(m+3)}\sim\sqrt{2m\,L(m)}$).
nodes.name: Medium part is negligible
nodes.label: lem:hw_medium

nodes.statement:
Put $a_j:=\sqrt{2\,j\,L(j)}$, positive nondecreasing with $a_j\to\infty$. The partial
sums of the independent, mean-zero terms $(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\E Y_j^{\mathrm M})/a_{j+1}$
form an $L^2$-bounded martingale, since by independence and Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_medium_var}
\[
  \int\Big(\sum_{j<n}\tfrac{Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\E Y_j^{\mathrm M}}{a_{j+1}}\Big)^2
  =\sum_{j<n}\frac{\Var(Y_j^{\mathrm M})}{a_{j+1}^2}
  \le\tfrac12\sum_{j}\frac{\Var(Y_j^{\mathrm M})}{j\,L(j)}<\infty .
\]
Hence $\sum_j(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\E Y_j^{\mathrm M})/a_{j+1}$ converges a.s.\ by the $L^2$
martingale convergence theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:slln_l2_conv}), and Kronecker's lemma with
weights $b_j=a_j$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:kronecker_general}, whose conclusion
$a_m^{-1}\sum_{j<m}a_{j+1}y_j\to0$ with $y_j=(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\E Y_j^{\mathrm M})/a_{j+1}$
is exactly $a_m^{-1}\sum_{j<m}(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\E Y_j^{\mathrm M})\to0$) gives
$W_m=o(a_m)=o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$ a.s. This is the Kolmogorov-convergence-plus-Kronecker
pattern of the martingale SLLN (Chapter~\ref{chap:pre_slln}); both ingredients are
already formalized.
nodes.name: Proof of Medium part is negligible
nodes.statement_short: L2-bounded weighted martingale converges; Kronecker with weights a_j.

nodes.statement:
$|D_m|\le2\sigma^2\sqrt m$, so $D_m=O(\sqrt m)=o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$. (The formalized statement is the
deterministic core $|\sum_{j<m}\!\int\operatorname{trunc}(X,\sqrt j)|\le2(\int X^2)\sqrt m$ for a
single centred $X$; since the i.i.d.\ $Y_j$ share the law of $X$, $D_m=\sum_{j<m}\!\int
\operatorname{trunc}(X,\sqrt j)$ and this is exactly $|D_m|\le2\sigma^2\sqrt m$.)
nodes.name: Drift is negligible
nodes.label: lem:hw_drift

nodes.statement:
Each summand $\E[Y_j\indic_{\{|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}}]$ is the mean of the truncation of the
centred $Y_j$ at level $\sqrt j$, so the already-formalized centred truncated-mean bound
$|\!\int\operatorname{trunc}(X,A)|\le\E[X^2]/A$
(\texttt{AlphaRAR.abs\_integral\_truncation\_le}, about Mathlib's
\texttt{MeasureTheory.truncation}) gives $|\E[Y_j\indic_{\{|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}}]|\le
\sigma^2/\sqrt j$. Summing with $\sum_{j\le m}1/\sqrt j\le2\sqrt m$
(\texttt{AlphaRAR.sum\_one\_div\_sqrt\_le}, also formalized) gives $|D_m|\le2\sigma^2
\sqrt m$; and $\sqrt m/\sqrt{m\,L(m)}\to0$, so $D_m=o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$. Both cited bounds
are exactly those used for the drift in the existing (log-rate) truncation route
(Lemmas~\ref{lem:trunc_mean_bound}--\ref{lem:trunc_drift}), applied here at level
$\sqrt j$ instead of $\sqrt i$.
nodes.name: Proof of Drift is negligible
nodes.statement_short: Truncated-mean bound summed with sum of 1/sqrt(j) <= 2 sqrt(m).

nodes.statement:
For i.i.d.\ $(Y_j)$ with $\E[Y_1]=0$ and $0<\E[Y_1^2]=\sigma^2<\infty$, almost surely
\[
  \limsup_{m\to\infty}\frac{S_m}{\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,\log\log m}}\ \le\ 1,
\]
in particular $S_m=O(\sqrt{m\log\log m})$; the two-sided form follows from $-Y$.
nodes.name: i.i.d.\ Hartman--Wintner, upper half
nodes.statement_short: Upper half of the Hartman-Wintner LIL for i.i.d. sums with finite variance.
nodes.label: thm:hw

nodes.statement:
By Definition~\ref{def:hw_trunc}, $S_m=\tilde S_m+W_m+H_m+D_m$, and the three remainders
are $o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$: $H_m=O(1)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_high}), $W_m=o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_medium}) and $D_m=o(\sqrt m)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_drift}). Hence
$\limsup_m S_m/\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}=\limsup_m\tilde S_m/\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}\le1$
by the sharp low-part bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_low_H}). No $A_0\to0$ limit (as in
de~Acosta's LIL-scale truncation) is needed: the log-level cutoff $b_j\to\infty$ already
gives $\Var(Y_j^{\mathrm L})\to\sigma^2$, so the constant is sharp. The two-sided statement
applies this to $-Y$.

\emph{Formalization} (\texttt{AlphaRAR.iid\_hartmanWintner\_limsup\_le\_one}). Because Mathlib's
\texttt{truncation} is half-open $(-b_j,b_j]$, the pointwise identity $Y_j=Y_j^{\mathrm L}+
Y_j^{\mathrm M}+Y_j^{\mathrm H}$ fails only at the single boundary atom $\{Y_j=-b_j\}$, where the
uncovered mass is $-b_j\le0$; \emph{dropping} it gives the one-sided pointwise bound $Y_j\le
Y_j^{\mathrm L}+Y_j^{\mathrm M}+Y_j\indic_{\{|Y_j|>\sqrt j\}}$ (\texttt{le\_lowMedHigh}), enough for the
upper half. The drift picks up the atom in expectation, controlled by $\sum_j b_j\,\Prob(Y_j=-b_j)\le
\E|Y_0|<\infty$ (\texttt{sum\_atom\_le}, using that the distinct $-b_j$ index disjoint events).
A coboundedness-free core (\texttt{hw\_eventually}) proves ``a.s.\ $\forall\beta>1$ eventually
$S_m\le\beta\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}$''; applying it to $-Y$ gives the matching lower bound
$S_m\ge-\beta\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}$, which supplies the coboundedness needed to pass to the
$\limsup$. The nondegeneracy $\sigma^2>0$ is used so the weight is eventually positive.
nodes.name: Proof of i.i.d.\ Hartman--Wintner, upper half
nodes.statement_short: Three-level decomposition: remainders negligible, low part has the sharp LIL.

nodes.statement:
The bound $\limsup_m S_m/\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\log\log m}\le1$ can instead be obtained in one
stroke by de~Acosta's method \cite{deAcosta1983}, which avoids the three-level split and
may be cleaner to formalize as a self-contained i.i.d.\ result. In that route
Theorem~\ref{thm:hw} is proved directly, while the general Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_general}
is still used for the genuinely martingale (bounded or \textbf{(H)}) applications ---
notably the assignment martingale $M_{\cdot,k}$.
nodes.name: de~Acosta's one-shot alternative
nodes.label: rem:hw_deacosta

nodes.statement:
Consider an algorithm--environment sequence $(A_j,Y_j)_{j\ge0}$ in a stationary environment with
per-arm reward kernel $\nu$: the response $Y_j$ is drawn from $\nu(A_j)$, independent of the history
given the current arm (the action-augmented filtration $\filt_{j-1}\vee\sigma(A_j)$). Fix an arm $k$
pulled infinitely often a.s., and let $\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots$ enumerate the pulls $\{j:A_j=k\}$. Then
the sampled responses $(Y_{\tau_m})_{m\ge0}$ are i.i.d.\ with law $\nu_k$.
nodes.section: 13.6 Optional skipping and the response martingale
nodes.name: Optional skipping
nodes.statement_short: Responses sampled at the pull times of a fixed arm are i.i.d. with that arm's law.
assumptions: Fix an arm $k$ pulled infinitely often a.s.
conclusions: the sampled responses $(Y_{\tau_m})_{m\ge0}$ are i.i.d.\ with law $\nu_k$
nodes.label: lem:opt_skip

nodes.statement:
The classical optional-skipping argument, with the selector $D_j=\indic_{\{A_j=k\}}$. Decompose over
the value $j$ of the $m$-th pull time $\tau_m$: the event $\{\tau_m=j\}$ coincides a.s.\ with the
predictable hit event $\{N_j=m,\ A_j=k\}$ (where $N_j=\#\{i<j:A_i=k\}$), which is measurable for the
action-augmented $\sigma$-algebra at time $j$, and on it the conditional law of $Y_j$ is the constant
$\nu_k$ (\texttt{condExp\_feedback}). Hence, for any prefix and measurable sets $E_i$,
$\Prob\!\big(\bigcap_{i<N}Y_{\tau_i}^{-1}E_i\big)=\prod_{i<N}\nu_k(E_i)$ by induction on $N$, peeling
the newest sample and summing over its a.s.-covering, pairwise-disjoint pull events; this is
independence together with each marginal $=\nu_k$.

\emph{Formalization.} The combinatorial core is generic (\texttt{AlphaRAR.iIndepFun\_sampledSeq},
\texttt{map\_sampledSeq\_eq}): for a predictable $\{0,1\}$-selector $D$ and a process $Y$ whose value
is $\rho$-fresh given the current $\sigma$-algebra on $\{D_j=1\}$
(\texttt{hfact}: $\mu(Y_j^{-1}E\cap S)=\rho(E)\,\mu(S)$ for $S\subseteq\{D_j=1\}$), the samples at the
hit times of $D$ are i.i.d.\ $\rho$. The hit time $\tau_m$ is \texttt{Nat.nth}, and the honestly
$\sigma$-algebra-measurable hit events replace the (absent from Mathlib) random stopping-time
$\sigma$-algebra. The freshness \texttt{hfact} is discharged for the response process
(\texttt{hfact\_stationaryEnv}) from the stationary-environment conditional distribution. This
general statement is not yet in Mathlib and is a worthwhile contribution.
nodes.section: 13.6 Optional skipping and the response martingale
nodes.name: Proof of Optional skipping
nodes.statement_short: Decompose over the pull-time values; freshness of responses gives a product formula by induction.

nodes.statement:
In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:opt_skip}, write $D_j=\indic_{\{A_j=k\}}$, let $\theta_k$ be the
mean of $\nu_k$ and $N_n=\sum_{j<n}D_j$ (the number of pulls of arm $k$ before $n$). If
$\Var(\nu_k)=V<\infty$, then almost surely
\[
  \Big|\sum_{j<n}D_j(Y_j-\theta_k)\Big|\ =\ O\!\big(\sqrt{N_n\,\log\log N_n}\big).
\]
nodes.section: 13.6 Optional skipping and the response martingale
nodes.name: LIL for a predictably-sampled i.i.d.\ sum
nodes.statement_short: LIL bound for the response martingale via optional skipping and Hartman-Wintner.
nodes.label: cor:subsampled_lil

nodes.statement:
Reindexing the nonzero summands, $\sum_{j<n}D_j(Y_j-\theta_k)=S_{N_n}$ with
$S_m:=\sum_{i<m}(Y_{\tau_i}-\theta_k)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:opt_skip} the $(Y_{\tau_i})$ are i.i.d.\ with
law $\nu_k$, so $S$ is an i.i.d.\ centred sum with variance $V$; since $N_n\to\infty$ a.s.,
Theorem~\ref{thm:hw} (two-sided) gives $|S_{N_n}|=O(\sqrt{N_n\log\log N_n})$.

\emph{Formalization} (\texttt{AlphaRAR.abs\_respMart\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_loglog}). The formalized
statement is the sharp two-sided form: a.s., for every $\beta>1$, eventually
$|Q_{n,k}|\le\beta\sqrt{2V\,N_{n,k}\log\log N_{n,k}}$. The reindexing $Q_{n,k}=S_{N_{n,k}}$
(\texttt{respMart\_eq\_sum\_sampledSeq}) is an exact pointwise identity proved by induction on $n$
(a pull advances the sample rank via \texttt{Nat.nth\_count}). Hartman--Wintner is applied through
the coboundedness-free \emph{eventually} core (\texttt{hw\_eventually}) to the centred samples and
their negatives; the time-change $N_{n,k}\to\infty$ (\texttt{hitCount\_tendsto\_atTop}) transports
the eventual bound. The i.i.d.\ hypotheses and law $\nu_k$ of the samples come from
Lemma~\ref{lem:opt_skip}; the moments are transported to $\nu_k$ by change of variables. Requires
$\int x\,d\nu_k$, $\int x^2\,d\nu_k$ finite and $V=\Var(\nu_k)>0$.
nodes.section: 13.6 Optional skipping and the response martingale
nodes.name: Proof of LIL for a predictably-sampled i.i.d.\ sum
nodes.statement_short: Reindex as an i.i.d. sum evaluated at the count and apply Hartman-Wintner.

nodes.statement:
\textbf{Application.} This is the shape used in Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_LIL}: with
$Y_j=\xi_{j,k}$, $\theta=\theta_k$, $D_j=X_{j,k}$, and $N_n=N_{n,k}$, it yields
$Q_{n,k}=O(\sqrt{N_{n,k}\log\log N_{n,k}})$ a.s., the $\log\log$ upgrade of the
$Q$-bound. The bounded assignment martingale $M_{\cdot,k}$ instead goes through
Corollary~\ref{cor:llil_nat} (Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_bounded}), as it is genuinely
adaptive rather than a subsampled i.i.d.\ sum.
nodes.section: 13.6 Optional skipping and the response martingale
nodes.name: Application of the subsampled LIL to Q
nodes.statement_short: The subsampled LIL gives the loglog bound on Q; the assignment martingale instead uses the bounded-increment LIL.

nodes.statement:
A \emph{martingale difference array} consists, for each $n\in\N$, of
\begin{itemize}
  \item a filtration $(\filt_{n,i})_{i\in\N}$ of $\Omega$, one per row $n$ (allowing
        the filtration to depend on the row costs nothing: every estimate below is
        internal to a single row, and the two cross-row limits
        $V_n\xrightarrow{\Prob}\sigma^2$, $L_n(\varepsilon)\xrightarrow{\Prob}0$ refer
        only to $P$; it is what lets the self-normalized and joint applications supply a
        different filtration for each normalization). Within a fixed row $n$ we
        abbreviate $\filt_i:=\filt_{n,i}$;
  \item a length $k_n\in\N$ and increments $\Delta_{n,i}:\Omega\to\R$ for $i<k_n$,
        with $\Delta_{n,i}$ measurable with respect to $\filt_{i+1}$, square
        integrable, and
        \[
          \E[\Delta_{n,i}\mid\filt_{i}] = 0 \quad\text{a.s.}
        \]
\end{itemize}
nodes.name: Martingale difference array
nodes.statement_short: Rows of square-integrable increments adapted to per-row filtrations with zero conditional mean.

nodes.statement:
We write
$S_n := \sum_{i<k_n}\Delta_{n,i}$ for the row sum, and introduce the per-step
conditional variances and the predictable quadratic variation
\[
  v_{n,i} := \E[\Delta_{n,i}^2\mid\filt_{i}], \qquad
  V_n := \sum_{i<k_n} v_{n,i} \;=\; \langle M_n\rangle_{k_n},
\]
and, for $\varepsilon>0$, the \emph{conditional Lindeberg quantity}
\[
  L_n(\varepsilon) := \sum_{i<k_n}
    \E\!\big[\Delta_{n,i}^2\,\indic_{\{|\Delta_{n,i}|>\varepsilon\}}\mid\filt_{i}\big].
\]
nodes.name: Row sum, conditional variances and Lindeberg quantity
nodes.statement_short: Row sum, per-step conditional variances, predictable variation and conditional Lindeberg quantity of the array.

nodes.statement:
For all $x\in\R$,
\[
  \Big\| e^{ix} - \big(1 + ix - \tfrac{x^2}{2}\big)\Big\|
  \;\le\; \min\!\big(2x^2,\ |x|^3\big).
\]
nodes.name: Complex exponential expansion
nodes.label: lem:clt_exp_bound

nodes.statement:
Both bounds follow from a short integral tower for the map $x\mapsto e^{ix}$,
using $\tfrac{d}{dx}e^{ix}=ie^{ix}$ and the fundamental theorem of calculus.
First $\|e^{ix}-1\|=\|\int_0^x i e^{is}\,ds\|\le|x|$. Integrating,
$\|e^{ix}-1-ix\|=\|\int_0^x i(e^{is}-1)\,ds\|\le\int_0^{|x|}s\,ds=x^2/2$.
Integrating once more,
$\|e^{ix}-1-ix+\tfrac{x^2}{2}\|=\|\int_0^x i(e^{is}-1-is)\,ds\|
\le\int_0^{|x|}\tfrac{s^2}{2}\,ds=|x|^3/6$, which is the cubic bound. The
quadratic bound is $\|e^{ix}-1-ix\|+\tfrac{x^2}{2}\le x^2/2+x^2/2=x^2$.
The specific constant $1/6$ is not used downstream; any fixed constant on the
cubic term suffices.
nodes.name: Proof of Complex exponential expansion
nodes.statement_short: Integral tower for e^{ix} via the fundamental theorem of calculus.

nodes.statement: For every $y\ge0$, $\ \big|e^{y}(1-y)-1\big|\le y^2 e^{y}$.
nodes.name: A real elementary bound, unbounded form
nodes.label: lem:clt_real_exp_bound_pos

nodes.statement:
As above $\big|e^{y}(1-y)-1\big|=g(y)=1-e^{y}(1-y)\ge0$. Since $1-y+y^2\ge0$ and
$e^{y}\ge1+y$, we get $e^{y}(1-y+y^2)\ge(1+y)(1-y+y^2)=1+y^3\ge1$, i.e.
$e^{y}(1-y)+y^2e^{y}\ge1$, which rearranges to $g(y)\le y^2 e^{y}$. This form is
valid for all $y\ge0$ (not only $y\le1$); the factor $e^{y}$ is what is needed when
$y=\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,i}$ is only known to be bounded, not $\le1$.
nodes.name: Proof of A real elementary bound, unbounded form
nodes.statement_short: Elementary inequalities e^y >= 1 + y and 1 - y + y^2 >= 0.

nodes.statement:
Fix $t\in\R$. For each $n,i$ write
\[
  r_{n,i} := \E\big[e^{it\Delta_{n,i}}\mid\filt_i\big]
             - \Big(1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}\,v_{n,i}\Big).
\]
Then $\E[e^{it\Delta_{n,i}}\mid\filt_i] = 1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,i} + r_{n,i}$
with
\[
  \|r_{n,i}\| \;\le\;
  \E\!\Big[\min\!\big(2t^2\Delta_{n,i}^2,\ |t|^3|\Delta_{n,i}|^3\big)
    \,\Big|\,\filt_i\Big].
\]
nodes.name: Conditional characteristic increment
nodes.label: lem:clt_cond_char

nodes.statement:
Apply the conditional expectation to the pointwise identity
$e^{it\Delta} = 1 + it\Delta - \tfrac{t^2}{2}\Delta^2
 + \big(e^{it\Delta}-1-it\Delta+\tfrac{t^2}{2}\Delta^2\big)$. The linear term
vanishes since $\E[\Delta_{n,i}\mid\filt_i]=0$ (conditional expectation commutes
with the coercion $\R\to\mathbb{C}$), and the quadratic term is $-\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,i}$ by
definition of $v_{n,i}$. The remainder $r_{n,i}$ is the conditional expectation of
the last bracket, whose modulus is bounded pointwise by
$\min(2t^2\Delta^2,\,|t|^3|\Delta|^3)$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_exp_bound} applied to
$x=t\Delta$; conditional Jensen (\texttt{norm\_condExp\_le}) gives the stated bound.
nodes.name: Proof of Conditional characteristic increment
nodes.statement_short: Second-order expansion of e^{it Delta} under conditional expectation; conditional Jensen bounds the remainder.

nodes.statement:
Fix a constant $B$ with $\sigma^2<B$ (e.g.\ $B:=\sigma^2+1$). Define the stopped
array by truncating increment $i$ as soon as the \emph{next} partial variance
would exceed $B$:
\[
  \bar\Delta_{n,i}:=\Delta_{n,i}\,\indic_{\{V_{n,i+1}\le B\}},
  \qquad V_{n,i+1}=\textstyle\sum_{l\le i}v_{n,l}.
\]
The indicator is $\filt_i$-measurable, since $V_{n,i+1}$ depends only on
$v_{n,0},\dots,v_{n,i}$, all $\filt_i$-measurable. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[(i)] $\bar\Delta_{n,i}$ is again a martingale difference array for
        $(\filt_i)$, with per-step variances
        $\bar v_{n,i}=v_{n,i}\indic_{\{V_{n,i+1}\le B\}}$;
  \item[(ii)] its predictable variation is bounded \emph{by the constant $B$}:
        $\bar V_n=\sum_{i<k_n}\bar v_{n,i}\le B$ everywhere;
  \item[(iii)] $\bar V_n\xrightarrow{\Prob}\sigma^2$, and $\bar\Delta_{n,i}$
        satisfies the conditional Lindeberg condition;
  \item[(iv)] $P\big(\bar S_n\ne S_n\big)\le P(V_n>B)\to0$, where
        $\bar S_n=\sum_{i<k_n}\bar\Delta_{n,i}$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $S_n$ and $\bar S_n$ have the same characteristic-function limit, and
it suffices to prove the theorem under the extra assumption $V_n\le B$ a.s.
nodes.name: Variance truncation
nodes.statement_short: Truncating increments once predictable variance exceeds B preserves the MDA and the limit.
nodes.label: lem:clt_truncation

nodes.statement:
Since $v_{n,l}$ is $\filt_l$-measurable and $l\le i$ for $l$ appearing in
$V_{n,i+1}$, the indicator $\indic_{\{V_{n,i+1}\le B\}}$ is $\filt_i$-measurable;
multiplying $\Delta_{n,i}$ by it therefore preserves both the $\filt_{i+1}$-
measurability and the martingale-difference property
($\E[\bar\Delta_{n,i}\mid\filt_i]=\indic_{\{V_{n,i+1}\le B\}}\E[\Delta_{n,i}\mid\filt_i]=0$),
and $\bar v_{n,i}=\E[\bar\Delta_{n,i}^2\mid\filt_i]=\indic_{\{V_{n,i+1}\le B\}}v_{n,i}$,
proving (i). For (ii): because $V$ is nondecreasing, the retained indices
$\{i:V_{n,i+1}\le B\}$ form a prefix $\{0,\dots,m\}$, and
$\bar V_n=\sum_{i\le m}v_{n,i}=V_{n,m+1}\le B$ by the choice of $m$ --- there is no
overshoot. For (iii): on $\{V_n\le B\}$ every indicator equals $1$, so $\bar
V_n=V_n$ and $\bar S_n=S_n$; since $P(V_n\le B)\to1$ (as
$V_n\xrightarrow{\Prob}\sigma^2<B$), both $\bar V_n\xrightarrow{\Prob}\sigma^2$ and
(iv) follow, and the Lindeberg sum only decreases under truncation
($\bar\Delta_{n,i}^2\le\Delta_{n,i}^2$, $\{|\bar\Delta|>\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{|\Delta|>\varepsilon\}$).
The final claim uses
$\|\charFun(\mathrm{law}\,S_n)(t)-\charFun(\mathrm{law}\,\bar S_n)(t)\|\le
2P(S_n\ne\bar S_n)$.
nodes.name: Proof of Variance truncation
nodes.statement_short: Measurability of the truncating indicator, monotonicity of V, and coupling on {V_n <= B}.

nodes.statement:
For every $\varepsilon>0$ and every $i<k_n$, a.s.
\[
  v_{n,i}\;\le\;\varepsilon^2 + L_n(\varepsilon).
\]
In particular $\max_{i<k_n} v_{n,i}\le\varepsilon^2 + L_n(\varepsilon)$, so
$L_n(\varepsilon)\xrightarrow{\Prob}0$ gives $\max_{i<k_n}v_{n,i}\xrightarrow{\Prob}0$.
nodes.name: Uniform smallness of the conditional variances
nodes.label: lem:clt_max_var

nodes.statement:
Split $v_{n,i}=\E[\Delta_{n,i}^2\indic_{\{|\Delta_{n,i}|\le\varepsilon\}}\mid\filt_i]
+\E[\Delta_{n,i}^2\indic_{\{|\Delta_{n,i}|>\varepsilon\}}\mid\filt_i]$. The first
conditional expectation is $\le\varepsilon^2$ (its integrand is $\le\varepsilon^2$
pointwise); the second is the $i$-th summand of $L_n(\varepsilon)$, hence
$\le L_n(\varepsilon)$ since every summand is nonnegative (conditional expectation
of a nonnegative function). The stated per-cell bound follows.
nodes.name: Proof of Uniform smallness of the conditional variances
nodes.statement_short: Split the conditional variance at level epsilon.

nodes.statement:
For every $\varepsilon>0$, a.s.
\[
  \sum_{i<k_n} v_{n,i}^2 \;\le\; \big(\varepsilon^2 + L_n(\varepsilon)\big)\,V_n .
\]
In particular, on $\{V_n\le B'\}$ with $L_n(\varepsilon)\xrightarrow{\Prob}0$, this
gives $\sum_{i<k_n}v_{n,i}^2\xrightarrow{\Prob}0$.
nodes.name: Sum of squared variances
nodes.label: lem:clt_sum_var_sq

nodes.name: Proof of Sum of squared variances
nodes.statement_short: Max bound times the sum.

nodes.statement:
For every $\varepsilon\ge0$, a.s.
\[
  \sum_{i<k_n}\E\!\big[\min(2t^2\Delta_{n,i}^2,\,|t|^3|\Delta_{n,i}|^3)\mid\filt_i\big]
  \;\le\; |t|^3\varepsilon\,V_n + 2t^2 L_n(\varepsilon).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_cond_char} the left-hand side dominates $\sum_{i<k_n}\|r_{n,i}\|$;
hence on $\{V_n\le B'\}$ with $L_n(\varepsilon)\xrightarrow{\Prob}0$,
$\sum_{i<k_n}\|r_{n,i}\|\xrightarrow{\Prob}0$ (send $n\to\infty$, then $\varepsilon\to0$).
nodes.name: Sum of the remainder majorants
nodes.label: lem:clt_sum_rem

nodes.statement:
Pointwise, $\min(2t^2\Delta^2,|t|^3|\Delta|^3)\le
|t|^3\varepsilon\,\Delta^2 + 2t^2\,\Delta^2\indic_{\{|\Delta|>\varepsilon\}}$: on
$\{|\Delta|\le\varepsilon\}$ use the cubic term ($|t|^3|\Delta|^3\le|t|^3\varepsilon\Delta^2$),
on $\{|\Delta|>\varepsilon\}$ the quadratic term. Taking conditional expectations
and summing over $i$ gives $|t|^3\varepsilon\sum_i v_{n,i}+2t^2 L_n(\varepsilon)$.
nodes.name: Proof of Sum of the remainder majorants
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise min bound split at epsilon, then conditional expectation.

nodes.statement:
Define the partial sums $S_{n,j}:=\sum_{i<j}\Delta_{n,i}$ and
$V_{n,j}:=\sum_{i<j}v_{n,i}$, and the complex process
\[
  Z_{n,j} := \exp\!\Big(i t\,S_{n,j} + \tfrac{t^2}{2}V_{n,j}\Big),
  \qquad j\le k_n .
\]
nodes.name: Exponential compensated process Z

nodes.statement:
Then $Z_{n,0}=1$, $\ |Z_{n,j}|=\exp(\tfrac{t^2}{2}V_{n,j})\le\exp(\tfrac{t^2}{2}B')$,
and $e^{itS_n}=Z_{n,k_n}\,\exp(-\tfrac{t^2}{2}V_n)$.
nodes.name: Basic properties of Z

nodes.statement: $\E[Z_{n,k_n}]\to1$ as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.name: Almost-martingale expectation
nodes.label: lem:clt_Z_expectation

nodes.statement:
The one-step increment factorises as
$Z_{n,j+1}-Z_{n,j}=Z_{n,j}\big(\exp(it\Delta_{n,j}+\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,j})-1\big)$,
where the factor $Z_{n,j}$ is $\filt_j$-measurable. Taking conditional
expectation and using Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_cond_char},
\[
  \E[Z_{n,j+1}-Z_{n,j}\mid\filt_j]
  = Z_{n,j}\Big(e^{(t^2/2)v_{n,j}}\big(1-\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,j}+r_{n,j}\big)-1\Big).
\]
Writing $y=\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,j}\ (\le\tfrac{t^2}{2}B')$, the bracket splits as
$\big(e^{y}(1-y)-1\big)+e^{y}r_{n,j}$; by
Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_real_exp_bound_pos}, $|e^{y}(1-y)-1|\le y^2 e^{y}
=\tfrac{t^4}{4}v_{n,j}^2\,e^{y}$. Hence the modulus is
$\le|Z_{n,j}|\,e^{(t^2/2)B'}\big(\tfrac{t^4}{4}v_{n,j}^2+\|r_{n,j}\|\big)$.
(The unbounded form of the elementary bound is essential here: $y$ is only bounded,
not $\le1$.) Summing over $j$, telescoping and using the tower property
$\E[Z_{n,k_n}-Z_{n,0}]=\sum_j\E\big[\E[Z_{n,j+1}-Z_{n,j}\mid\filt_j]\big]$,
\[
  \big|\E[Z_{n,k_n}]-1\big|
  \le e^{(t^2/2)B'}\,\E\!\Big[\tfrac{t^4}{4}\textstyle\sum_j v_{n,j}^2
      + e^{(t^2/2)B'}\sum_j\|r_{n,j}\|\Big].
\]
Both sums tend to $0$ in probability
(Lemmas~\ref{lem:clt_sum_var_sq},~\ref{lem:clt_sum_rem}) and are uniformly
bounded, so by bounded convergence the expectations tend to $0$.
nodes.name: Proof of Almost-martingale expectation
nodes.statement_short: Telescoping the almost-martingale Z with conditional increment bounds and bounded convergence.

nodes.statement:
Under the two hypotheses ($V_n\xrightarrow{\Prob}\sigma^2$ and the conditional
Lindeberg condition), for every $t\in\R$,
\[
  \E\big[e^{itS_n}\big]\;=\;\charFun(\mathrm{law}\,S_n)(t)
  \longrightarrow \exp\!\Big(-\tfrac{\sigma^2 t^2}{2}\Big).
\]
nodes.name: Characteristic function limit
nodes.label: lem:clt_product

nodes.statement:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_truncation} we may assume $V_n\le B'$ a.s. Then
$e^{itS_n}=Z_{n,k_n}e^{-(t^2/2)V_n}$, so
\[
  \E[e^{itS_n}] - \exp(-\tfrac{t^2}{2}\sigma^2)
  = \E\big[Z_{n,k_n}\big(e^{-(t^2/2)V_n}-e^{-(t^2/2)\sigma^2}\big)\big]
    + e^{-(t^2/2)\sigma^2}\big(\E[Z_{n,k_n}]-1\big).
\]
The second term $\to0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_Z_expectation}. In the first,
$|Z_{n,k_n}|\le e^{(t^2/2)B'}$ is bounded and
$e^{-(t^2/2)V_n}-e^{-(t^2/2)\sigma^2}\xrightarrow{\Prob}0$ (continuity of $\exp$
and $V_n\xrightarrow{\Prob}\sigma^2$), so bounded convergence gives $\to0$.
nodes.name: Proof of Characteristic function limit
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to bounded variance, factor e^{itS_n} through Z and use bounded convergence.

nodes.statement:
The map sending a probability measure to its characteristic function is injective,
and if $\E[e^{itX_n}]\to\exp(-\sigma^2 t^2/2)$ for all $t$, then $X_n$ converges in
distribution to $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$.
nodes.name: Characteristic functions determine the limit
nodes.label: lem:levy

nodes.statement:
The target $\exp(-\sigma^2 t^2/2)$ is the characteristic function of
$\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$ (\texttt{charFun\_gaussianReal}). Pointwise convergence
of characteristic functions to that of a fixed probability measure implies weak
convergence of the laws by the L\'evy continuity theorem
(\texttt{ProbabilityMeasure.tendsto\_of\_tendsto\_charFun}); injectivity is
\texttt{Measure.ext\_of\_charFun}. Together these give convergence in distribution
to $\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$.
nodes.name: Proof of Characteristic functions determine the limit
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian characteristic function plus Levy continuity in Mathlib.

nodes.statement:
Let $(\Delta_{n,i})_{i<k_n}$ be a martingale difference array (as in the standing
setup) with predictable quadratic variation $V_n\xrightarrow{\Prob}\sigma^2$ and
satisfying the conditional Lindeberg condition
$L_n(\varepsilon)\xrightarrow{\Prob}0$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. Then the row sums
converge in distribution,
\[
  S_n=\sum_{i<k_n}\Delta_{n,i} \;\eqdist\; \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2).
\]
In Lean the conclusion has the shape of Mathlib's i.i.d.\ central limit theorem: for every random
variable $Y$ (on any probability space) with law $\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$, $S_n$ converges to $Y$
in distribution (\texttt{TendstoInDistribution}); the convergence of the laws of $S_n$ themselves
is the case $Y=\mathrm{id}$ on $(\R,\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2))$.
nodes.name: Martingale CLT, Lindeberg form
nodes.statement_short: Lindeberg martingale CLT for triangular arrays with converging predictable variation.
nodes.label: thm:mart_clt

nodes.statement:
Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_product} gives pointwise convergence of the characteristic
functions to that of $\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$; Lemma~\ref{lem:levy} converts this
into convergence in distribution.
nodes.name: Proof of Martingale CLT, Lindeberg form
nodes.statement_short: Characteristic function limit plus Levy continuity.

nodes.statement:
Fix an arm $k$ with a limiting proportion $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k>0$ a.s.\ and per-step conditional
variance $V_k>0$ (a finite second moment $\E|\xi_{1,k}-\theta_k|^2 = V_k<\infty$). Then the
self-normalized response martingale converges in distribution,
\[
  \frac{Q_{n,k}}{\sqrt{V_k\,N_{n,k}}} \eqdist \mathcal N(0,1).
\]
nodes.name: Per-arm self-normalized CLT
nodes.label: lem:mart_clt_selfnorm_arm

nodes.statement:
Normalize $Q_{n,k}$ by the \emph{deterministic} $\sqrt{V_k v_k n}$: the increments
$\Delta_{m}=X_{m,k}(\xi_{m,k}-\theta_k)/\sqrt{V_k v_k n}$ form a martingale-difference array (for the
action-augmented filtration) whose predictable variation is $N_{n,k}/(v_k n)\xrightarrow{\Prob}1$
(consistency) and which satisfies the conditional Lindeberg condition, because the sampled responses
are i.i.d.\ with finite variance $V_k$ (each cell contributes
$\indic\{A_m=k\}\,V_k^{-1}v_k^{-1}n^{-1}\E[(\xi-\theta_k)^2\indic\{|\xi-\theta_k|>\varepsilon\sqrt{V_k v_k n}\}]$
and the truncated moment vanishes by dominated convergence). Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_clt} then gives
$Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{V_k v_k n}\eqdist\mathcal N(0,1)$. Finally
$\sqrt{V_k v_k n}/\sqrt{V_k N_{n,k}}=\sqrt{v_k n/N_{n,k}}\xrightarrow{\Prob}1$, so Slutsky yields the
stated random-normalizer limit.
nodes.name: Proof of Per-arm self-normalized CLT
nodes.statement_short: Deterministic normalization, martingale CLT, then Slutsky to the random normalizer.

nodes.statement:
Suppose $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ a.s.\ for every arm $k$, with $v_k\ge0$ and $V_k\ge0$. Then the vector of
deterministically-normalized response martingales converges jointly in distribution to a diagonal
Gaussian,
\[
  \Big(\tfrac{Q_{n,1}}{\sqrt n},\dots,\tfrac{Q_{n,K}}{\sqrt n}\Big)
    \eqdist \mathcal N\!\big(0, \mathrm{diag}(v_1V_1,\dots,v_KV_K)\big).
\]
nodes.name: Joint componentwise CLT, deterministic normalization
nodes.label: lem:mart_clt_joint

nodes.statement:
By the Cramér--Wold device it suffices to prove that every scalar projection converges: for each
$w\in\R^K$, $\langle w, Q_n/\sqrt n\rangle = \big(\sum_k w_k Q_{n,k}\big)/\sqrt n$. The increments
$\sum_k w_k X_{i,k}(\xi_{i,k}-\theta_k)$ form a single martingale-difference array (the arm indicators
are disjoint, so the conditional square is $\sum_k w_k^2\indic\{A_i=k\}V_k$, giving predictable
variation $\sum_k w_k^2 V_k N_{n,k}/n\to\sum_k w_k^2 v_kV_k$; the conditional Lindeberg condition
holds arm-by-arm by dominated convergence). Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_clt} yields
$\big(\sum_k w_k Q_{n,k}\big)/\sqrt n\eqdist\mathcal N(0,\sum_k w_k^2 v_kV_k)$, which is precisely the
projection $\langle w,\cdot\rangle$ of the diagonal Gaussian (whose covariance is
$\mathrm{diag}(v_kV_k)$ by orthogonality of the coordinates, Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_orthogonal}). Cramér--Wold
then gives the joint limit.
nodes.name: Proof of Joint componentwise CLT, deterministic normalization
nodes.statement_short: Cramer-Wold: each projection is a martingale array satisfying the CLT hypotheses.

nodes.statement:
Suppose $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ a.s.\ for every arm $k$, with $v_k>0$. Then, under
Condition~\textbf{A}, the vector of response martingales normalized by their own random counts
converges jointly in distribution to a diagonal Gaussian,
\[
  \Big(\tfrac{Q_{n,1}}{\sqrt{N_{n,1}}},\dots,\tfrac{Q_{n,K}}{\sqrt{N_{n,K}}}\Big)
    \eqdist \mathcal N\!\big(0, \mathrm{diag}(V_1,\dots,V_K)\big).
\]
nodes.name: Joint componentwise CLT, self-normalized
nodes.label: lem:mart_clt_joint_selfnorm

nodes.statement:
Write $Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}}=(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt n)\cdot\sqrt{n/N_{n,k}}$. The deterministic-normalizer
joint limit (Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_clt_joint}) gives
$(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt n)_k\eqdist\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{diag}(v_kV_k))$, and the coordinatewise scaling
vector $(\sqrt{n/N_{n,k}})_k\to(v_k^{-1/2})_k$ in probability (from $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ and
$v_k>0$). Multivariate Slutsky (a continuous coordinatewise product against a constant limit) then
sends the product to the image of $\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{diag}(v_kV_k))$ under the diagonal scaling
$\mathrm{diag}(v_k^{-1/2})$, which is $\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{diag}(V_k))$.
nodes.name: Proof of Joint componentwise CLT, self-normalized
nodes.statement_short: Deterministic-normalizer joint CLT and multivariate Slutsky with the scaling vector.

nodes.statement:
Suppose $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ a.s.\ with $v_k>0$ for every arm $k$ (so in particular
$N_{n,k}\to\infty$). Then, under Condition~\textbf{A}, with
$D_n=\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{N_{n,1}},\dots,\sqrt{N_{n,K}})$,
\[
  D_n(\estParams_n-\Params)\eqdist\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{diag}(V_1,\dots,V_K)).
\]
nodes.name: Self-normalized componentwise form
nodes.label: cor:mart_clt_componentwise

nodes.statement:
By the exact Bahadur identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:estimator_bahadur}),
$\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k=(Q_{n,k}+(\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k))/(N_{n,k}+1)$, so
\[
  \sqrt{N_{n,k}}(\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k)
    = \frac{Q_{n,k}}{\sqrt{N_{n,k}}}\cdot\frac{N_{n,k}}{N_{n,k}+1}
      + (\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k)\frac{\sqrt{N_{n,k}}}{N_{n,k}+1}.
\]
The self-normalized martingale vector $(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}})_k$ converges jointly to
$\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{diag}(V_k))$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_clt_joint_selfnorm}), while the two
coordinatewise scaling factors tend to $1$ and $0$ in probability (as $N_{n,k}\to\infty$).
Multivariate Slutsky (a continuous coordinatewise affine map against the constant limit $(1,0)$)
therefore leaves the Gaussian limit unchanged.
nodes.name: Proof of Self-normalized componentwise form
nodes.statement_short: Bahadur identity, joint self-normalized CLT and multivariate Slutsky.

nodes.statement:
Let $(\xi_i)_{i\ge0}$ be i.i.d.\ with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $v=\mathrm{Var}(\xi_0)$, and let
$S_m=\sum_{i<m}(\xi_i-\mu)$. Let $(\tau_n)$ be positive-integer random indices for which there is a
deterministic sequence $c_n\to\infty$ with $\tau_n/c_n\to1$ almost surely. Then
\[
  \frac{S_{\tau_n}}{\sqrt{\tau_n}}
    = \frac1{\sqrt{\tau_n}}\Big(\sum_{i<\tau_n}\xi_i-\tau_n\mu\Big)
  \;\eqdist\; \mathcal N(0,v).
\]
nodes.name: Anscombe random-time self-normalized CLT
assumptions: Let $(\xi_i)_{i\ge0}$ be i.i.d.\ with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $v=\mathrm{Var}(\xi_0)$
nodes.label: lem:anscombe_clt

nodes.statement:
Decompose
$S_{\tau_n}/\sqrt{\tau_n}=(S_{c_n}/\sqrt{c_n})\cdot\sqrt{c_n/\tau_n}+(S_{\tau_n}-S_{c_n})/\sqrt{\tau_n}$.
The base term $S_{c_n}/\sqrt{c_n}\eqdist\mathcal N(0,v)$ is the i.i.d.\ central limit theorem
(Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_clt}, in the form of the Lindeberg--L\'evy theorem) precomposed with the
deterministic subsequence $c_n$; the scaling $\sqrt{c_n/\tau_n}\to1$ in probability by regularity, so
Slutsky preserves the limit; and the window remainder $(S_{\tau_n}-S_{c_n})/\sqrt{\tau_n}\to0$ in
probability, since on the event $|\tau_n-c_n|\le\varepsilon c_n$ (of probability $\to1$) the increment
is bounded by the maximal increment over a window of length $\varepsilon c_n$, which is
$O(\sqrt{\varepsilon c_n})$ in $L^1$ by Doob's maximal inequality; letting $\varepsilon\to0$ gives the
claim.

\emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.tendstoInDistribution\_anscombe\_iid}, assembled from the
base CLT along a subsequence (\texttt{tendstoInDistribution\_clt\_comp}, wrapping Mathlib's
\texttt{tendstoInDistribution\_inv\_sqrt\_mul\_sum\_sub}), the negligibility of the window remainder
(\texttt{AlphaRAR.tendstoInMeasure\_window}, via the Doob maximal inequality
\texttt{AlphaRAR.mart\_maximal} on the i.i.d.-sum martingale \texttt{AlphaRAR.martingale\_iidSum}),
and two Slutsky steps (\texttt{TendstoInDistribution.mul\_of\_tendstoInMeasure\_const},
Mathlib's \texttt{TendstoInDistribution.add\_of\_tendstoInMeasure\_const}). The regularity
$\tau_n/c_n\to1$ is
essential: for a general adaptive $\tau_n\to\infty$ the statement is false (one can freeze the
self-normalized martingale above its typical value by pausing the index near a level crossing, using
the law of the iterated logarithm). This lemma is the standalone martingale-CLT ingredient that
Lemma~\ref{lem:componentwise} calls for, and the missing piece for the sparse componentwise CLT
(Corollary~\ref{cor:sparse_clt}): with the per-arm regularity $N_{n,k}/c_{n,k}\to1$ supplied, applying
it coordinatewise to the sampled response martingale $Q_{\cdot,k}$ yields
$Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}}\eqdist\mathcal N(0,V_k)$ even when $v_k=0$.
nodes.name: Proof of Anscombe random-time self-normalized CLT
nodes.statement_short: Decompose into a deterministic-index CLT term, a scaling factor and a negligible window remainder.

nodes.statement:
Fix an arm $k$ sampled infinitely often, and suppose its pull count obeys the regularity
$N_{n,k}/c_n\to1$ a.s.\ for some deterministic $c_n\to\infty$. Then, under Condition~\textbf{A},
\[
  \frac{Q_{n,k}}{\sqrt{N_{n,k}}} \eqdist \mathcal N(0, V_k),\qquad V_k=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\mathrm{id};\nu_k].
\]
No positivity of a limiting proportion is required, so this holds for sparse arms $v_k=0$.
nodes.name: Per-arm self-normalized CLT, sparse
nodes.label: lem:mart_clt_selfnorm_arm_sparse

nodes.statement:
The sampled responses of arm $k$ are i.i.d.\ with mean $\theta_k$ and variance $V_k$
(a globally i.i.d.\ representative is \texttt{AlphaRAR.sampledClean}), and reindexing the pulls gives
$Q_{n,k}=\sum_{i<N_{n,k}}(\xi_i-\theta_k)=S_{N_{n,k}}$ (\texttt{respMart\_eq\_sum\_sampledSeq}). Apply
the Anscombe random-time CLT (Lemma~\ref{lem:anscombe_clt}) with $\tau_n=N_{n,k}$.

\emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.respMart\_selfNorm\_anscombe\_tendsto}: the clean-sample setup
mirrors the LIL development (\texttt{iIndepFun\_sampledResponse}, \texttt{map\_sampledResponse\_eq},
\texttt{sampledSeq\_ae\_eq\_sampledClean}), supplying the i.i.d.\ hypotheses of
Lemma~\ref{lem:anscombe_clt}, and the almost-everywhere identity
$S_{N_{n,k}}=Q_{n,k}$ transfers the limit law to $(\sqrt{N_{n,k}})^{-1}Q_{n,k}$.
nodes.name: Proof of Per-arm self-normalized CLT, sparse
nodes.statement_short: Reindex the response martingale as an i.i.d. sum at the count and apply Anscombe.

nodes.statement:
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_clt_selfnorm_arm_sparse},
$\sqrt{N_{n,k}}\,(\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k)\eqdist\mathcal N(0,V_k)$. This is the componentwise
statement of Corollary~\ref{cor:sparse_clt}.
nodes.name: Per-arm estimator CLT, sparse
nodes.label: lem:clt_theta_arm_sparse

nodes.statement:
By the exact Bahadur identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:estimator_bahadur}),
$\sqrt{N_{n,k}}(\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k)=(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}})\cdot\frac{N_{n,k}}{N_{n,k}+1}
 + (\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k)\frac{\sqrt{N_{n,k}}}{N_{n,k}+1}$; the scaling factors tend to $1$ and $0$
in probability (as $N_{n,k}\to\infty$), and Slutsky applied to
Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_clt_selfnorm_arm_sparse} gives the claim.

\emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.estimator\_sqrtN\_anscombe\_tendsto}, from
\texttt{respMart\_selfNorm\_anscombe\_tendsto} via \texttt{estimator\_sub\_eq} and the two Slutsky
